paragraphs.text: XII.A. Emergency Descent
Introduction
How
Basics 											AI.XII.A.K1, AI.XII.A.K2
Objective: Descend as soon and as rapidly as possible, within the structural limitations of the airplane
Emergency Descent Situations
Fire, smoke, loss of cabin pressure, or any other demanding situation (medical, injury, etc.)
POH 								  	     AI.XII.A.K3, AI.XII.A.K4, AI.XII.A.K5
Follow the procedures outlined in the POH
Review immediate action/memory items
Reference & note any applicable aircraft limitations
VNE, VLE, VFE, VA in turbulent air
Performance: Expected rate of descent at target airspeed(s)
Review any associated performance charts
Emergency Descent Procedures 								AI.XII.A.K1
Prior to the Maneuver
Pre-maneuver checklist; Clear the area
Procedure
Reduce power to idle
Configuration 										AI.XII.A.R3
Extend the flaps and gear as specified by the manufacturer
Provides maximum drag to increase the rate of descent, without excessive airspeed
Set the propeller to the low pitch (high rpm) setting
Lower the nose to maintain maximum allowable airspeed
Speed may vary based on flaps, nature of the emergency, and turbulent conditions
Don’t exceed VNE or VFE, and in the case of turbulence, do not exceed VA
As the nose is lowered, begin a 90o turn at 30-45o of bank
Puts positive load on the aircraft (countering the negative load from the descent)
Acts as a clearing turn (below and to each side) and gets the plane off an airway
Technique: Left turn because faster traffic passes on the right (right of way rules)
Level Off
The recovery should be smooth to prevent overstressing the airplane
These recommendations generally work well, but in the case of a real-life emergency descent (i.e., a fire in the cabin), do what is necessary to land safely & stay alive
Initiate the level off at an altitude that will ensure a safe recovery or precautionary landing
10% rule works well (lead the level off by 10% of the VSI)
Increase power to the cruise setting, or as required
Once straight-and-level, return to a normal configuration (flaps, gear, etc. are retracted)
Trim the aircraft and adjust the mixture as necessary
RM: Descent Factors 										AI.XII.A.R1
Altitude
Dictates the amount of descent
Recommended to level at/below 10,000’ in case of depressurization, safety permitting
In the case of an engine failure, altitude will dictate the distance the aircraft can travel
Wind
Headwind decreases the distance traveled; Tailwind increases the distance traveled
Becomes much more important in the case of an engine failure
Landing
Maximum Demonstrated Crosswind Component
Tailwind increases landing distance, verify performance (comply with limitations, exception: emergency)
Terrain & Obstructions
Preflight planning: Study and know terrain on the route and safe altitudes/max elevation figures
Be familiar with and especially cautious of terrain & obstructions during an emergency descent
Glide Distance
In the case the engine fails, and the aircraft must glide to the landing area
The farther the emergency descent is extended, the less glide distance available
Terminate the emergency descent at an altitude that ensures a precautionary or emergency landing
Know glide distance data and transition to the engine failure emergency landing
Common Errors										AI.XII.A.K6
The consequences of failing to identify reason for executing an emergency descent
Improper use of the prescribed emergency checklist to verify accomplishment of procedures for initiating the emergency descent
Improper use of clearing procedures for initiating the emergency descent
Improper procedures for recovering from an emergency descent
RM: Hazards
Collision Hazards 										AI.XII.A.R2
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program)
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
Pertinent to emergencies: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Be cautious, other aircraft may not know you’re in distress
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Research obstacles in the area - Charts, NOTAMs, Terminal procedures, etc.
Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL and support guy wires can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots frequently follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.XII.A.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem and fix it
Especially important to avoid distractions in an emergency with numerous tasks to manage
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
High task load during an emergency can lead to a loss of SA
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning - Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Emergency Descent: Maintain SA in relation to the level-off altitude, emergency & associated procedures, airplane configuration, and the plan (diversion)
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention for more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Organization is especially important in situations like this – many tasks, little time
“Attack the closest alligator”
When tasks are piling up, handle the most threatening problem
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

WHAT
An emergency descent is a maneuver for descending as rapidly as possible to a lower altitude, or to the ground for an emergency landing.

WHY
The need for this maneuver may result from an uncontrollable fire, a sudden loss of cabin pressurization, or any other situation demanding an immediate and rapid descent for survival.

paragraphs.text: XII.B. Emergency Approach & Landing
Introduction
How
Best Glide Speed 								            AI.XII.B.K2, AI.XII.B.K2a
Airspeed at which the aircraft glides the furthest for the least altitude lost in non-powered flight
Occurs at the highest lift-to-drag ratio (L/DMAX)
Glide Ratio: Distance the airplane travels in relation to the altitude it loses
Provides an estimate of how far you can fly
Any increase or decrease from best glide reduces the glide ratio
Best Glide & Weight
L/D determines the distance the airplane can glide, not weight
If the proper speed is maintained, changes in weight don’t affect the best glide angle or distance flown
However, a heavier plane needs to fly at a higher airspeed to obtain the same glide ratio
Best Glide & Wind 										AI.XII.B.K2c
With a tailwind, the airplane glides farther because of the higher groundspeed
With a headwind, the airplane does not glide as far because of the lower groundspeed
Best Glide & Configuration
When drag increases, the airplane must be pitched down to maintain airspeed (no longer at L/D max)
To maximize distance traveled, minimize drag-producing components
Minimum Sink Speed 										AI.XII.B.K2b
Airspeed used to maximize the time that the airplane remains in flight
Results in losing altitude at the lowest rate (lowest vertical speed)
Less distance traveled versus best glide airspeed
Not often published but generally a few knots less than best glide airspeed
Cardinal Rule: Do not attempt to “stretch” a glide by increasing back pressure/slowing below best glide
Any speed other than best glide reduces distance traveled
ABCD Checklist 										AI.XII.B.K1
AVIATE: The first reaction should be to immediately establish the best glide airspeed and fly the airplane
Flying the airplane is the most important priority
Variations in speed nullify accuracy in judgment of gliding distance / landing spot
Eagerness to get down is one of the most common faults during simulated emergency landings
Pilots neglect speed, arriving too fast for a safe landing – just as dangerous as too slow
BEST Landing Spot: Select the best landing spot and immediately turn toward it
Check in front, behind and to both sides of the airplane
Landing sites are restricted by the route of flight, height above the ground, and excess airspeed
An airport is ideal. If there is no airport, select a field within glide distance:
Preferably hard packed, long, smooth, with no obstacles, especially at the approach end
As a general rule, the pilot should not change their mind more than once
Note wind direction / speed; land into the wind, if able (altitude, obstacles, etc. may prevent this)
Be aware of tailwind (longer landing distance) and crosswinds
Always continue to clear for traffic
Emergency CHECKLISTs
Restart Checklist
Troubleshoot (if the reason for failure can be determined, a restart becomes more likely)
Check the systems to decipher the problem
DISTRESS Call
When able, inform ATC or Guard
Emergency Approach
Governed by:
Wind direction and speed
Dimensions and slope of the field
Obstacles on final approach path
Proceed directly to the landing area
Goal: Be on downwind, abeam the landing point at normal pattern altitude
If above pattern altitude, circle over the approach end while descending (steep spiral)
Turn in the same direction you intend to fly the pattern
RM: Following or changing the flight path to the landing area 				AI.XII.B.R2
Adjust as conditions change
Best practice is to go directly to the landing area & circle overhead, with a plan to enter the pattern
Divide attention between flying / checklists
Constantly assess the approach
Adjust the pattern based on altitude, wind, etc. to safely reach the landing area 		AI.XII.B.K3
Make the approach as normal as possible
Base & final turns are positioned based on altitude, wind, obstructions, etc.
Strong headwind = closer base Tailwind = farther out base
If high, delay base leg; if low, turn early, or go direct to landing area
If too high, consider:
Extending the pattern
S-turns
Configuring early
Slipping
If too low, consider:
Tightening the pattern
Proceeding directly to the landing area
Delaying configuration
Maintaining best glide
Stable Approach 										AI.XII.B.K4
The more stable the approach, the more predictable the approach
Maintain best glide, and attempt to make the approach as normal as possible
Flying the airplane is the highest priority
Energy Management
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management for more detailed energy management concepts - Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Configuration 											AI.XII.B.R4
Intent is to touchdown in a normal landing configuration (emergency permitting)
Flaps will be gradually lowered based on the conditions, situation, airplane performance, etc.
Have a standard position to lower the flaps and adjust based on the situation
Too high: Configure earlier (or delay configuration and slip, vary the base leg, etc.)
Too low: Delay configuration (tighten the base leg and/or turn to final)
Once flaps are lowered, they should not be retracted
Landing flaps should only be lowered once the landing area is assured
Contacting ATC
If on frequency with ATC, transmit “Mayday, mayday, mayday.” If not on frequency, use guard 121.5
Let them know who you are, where you are, and what you’re doing
The radios will likely be kept on until just before landing. Keep ATC apprised of the situation / plan
If time and conditions permit, squawk emergency - 7700
ATC Emergency Services 									AI.XII.B.K6
Priority: The frequency is basically yours, whatever you need
Aircraft Separation: Any other potentially hazardous aircraft will be moved out of your way
Advice: Nearby airports, etc.
Emergency Response: ATC will coordinate with the tower or local emergency response
Landing
If a restart is not an option, complete the Emergency Landing Checklist
Keep the electrical equipment on as long as practical to make radio calls, use the flaps, etc.
Gear & Flaps
Gear and flaps should only be lowered after landing is assured
Gear can provide better protection in the case of stumps, rocks, or other obstacles
If the field is excessively soft, wet, short, or snow covered, a gear up landing may be safer
If practical, hold the wheels off to allow for a gentle touchdown, like a soft field landing
At this point, the safety of the passengers is the only concern, the airplane does not matter
RM: Descent Factors 										AI.XII.B.R1
Altitude
Dictates the distance the aircraft can travel (use AGL, not MSL)
Know approximate distance traveled at best glide per 1,000’ – apply to the situation
The goal is to put the aircraft at a normal pattern altitude at a normal key position
Wind
During the approach
It can influence glide distance (headwind vs tailwind vs crosswind)
The stronger the wind on final, the closer the base leg needs to be to make a normal approach
Tailwind
A tailwind increases the runway required for landing
Maximum Demonstrated Crosswind Component
If possible, don’t exceed it as the aircraft may not be able to remain with the confines of the runway
Terrain & Obstructions
Be especially cautious of terrain/obstructions during an emergency approach & landing
Without an engine, there may not be enough energy to clear the terrain
Available Landing Distance
Be familiar with the landing distance needed for an emergency approach & pick a suitable landing area
Landing distance at off airport landing areas will have to be estimated from the air
Emergency Locating Devices (ELT)								AI.XII.B.K5
ELT: Small, self-contained transmitter that will automatically, upon impact, transmit an emergency signal
Transmits the emergency signal on 121.5, 243, and/or 406 MHz
Numerous private companies produce emergency locating devices that can be carried on oneself
Basic Personal Locator Beacons (PLBs)
Satellite Messengers
Mental Attitude
The survival records favor pilots who maintain their composure and know how to apply the concepts and procedures developed through the years. Success is as much a matter of the mind as of skills
“We don’t rise to the level of our expectations; we fall to the level of our training”
Common Errors 										AI.XII.B.K7
Improper airspeed control
Poor judgment in the selection of an emergency landing area
Failure to estimate the approximate wind speed and direction
Failure to fly the most suitable pattern for existing situation
Failure to accomplish the emergency checklist
Undershooting or overshooting selected emergency landing area
RM: Hazards
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.XII.B.R5
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Quick, panicked maneuvers can result in a stall or loss of control close to the ground
Especially important in engine failure emergencies
Be aware of, and avoid, obstructions, towers, etc.
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
During engine failures, maintain best glide – Stalls could be catastrophic low/without power
At low level, recover at any indication of a stall then adjust to make the emergency landing
Spin (Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries - follow POH procedures)
A spin is a result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Maintain coordination – don’t cross the controls especially during an emergency landing
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Stop whatever you’re doing and recover at the first sign of a stall
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
Once the spin has stopped, neutralize the rudders and raise the nose - be careful not to stall
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain): AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists & know your aircraft and equipment

standard_lessons.full_text:
XII.B. Emergency Approach & Landing
Introduction
How
Best Glide Speed 								            AI.XII.B.K2, AI.XII.B.K2a
Airspeed at which the aircraft glides the furthest for the least altitude lost in non-powered flight
Occurs at the highest lift-to-drag ratio (L/DMAX)
Glide Ratio: Distance the airplane travels in relation to the altitude it loses
Provides an estimate of how far you can fly
Any increase or decrease from best glide reduces the glide ratio
Best Glide & Weight
L/D determines the distance the airplane can glide, not weight
If the proper speed is maintained, changes in weight don’t affect the best glide angle or distance flown
However, a heavier plane needs to fly at a higher airspeed to obtain the same glide ratio
Best Glide & Wind 										AI.XII.B.K2c
With a tailwind, the airplane glides farther because of the higher groundspeed
With a headwind, the airplane does not glide as far because of the lower groundspeed
Best Glide & Configuration
When drag increases, the airplane must be pitched down to maintain airspeed (no longer at L/D max)
To maximize distance traveled, minimize drag-producing components
Minimum Sink Speed 										AI.XII.B.K2b
Airspeed used to maximize the time that the airplane remains in flight
Results in losing altitude at the lowest rate (lowest vertical speed)
Less distance traveled versus best glide airspeed
Not often published but generally a few knots less than best glide airspeed
Cardinal Rule: Do not attempt to “stretch” a glide by increasing back pressure/slowing below best glide
Any speed other than best glide reduces distance traveled
ABCD Checklist 										AI.XII.B.K1
AVIATE: The first reaction should be to immediately establish the best glide airspeed and fly the airplane
Flying the airplane is the most important priority
Variations in speed nullify accuracy in judgment of gliding distance / landing spot
Eagerness to get down is one of the most common faults during simulated emergency landings
Pilots neglect speed, arriving too fast for a safe landing – just as dangerous as too slow
BEST Landing Spot: Select the best landing spot and immediately turn toward it
Check in front, behind and to both sides of the airplane
Landing sites are restricted by the route of flight, height above the ground, and excess airspeed
An airport is ideal. If there is no airport, select a field within glide distance:
Preferably hard packed, long, smooth, with no obstacles, especially at the approach end
As a general rule, the pilot should not change their mind more than once
Note wind direction / speed; land into the wind, if able (altitude, obstacles, etc. may prevent this)
Be aware of tailwind (longer landing distance) and crosswinds
Always continue to clear for traffic
Emergency CHECKLISTs
Restart Checklist
Troubleshoot (if the reason for failure can be determined, a restart becomes more likely)
Check the systems to decipher the problem
DISTRESS Call
When able, inform ATC or Guard
Emergency Approach
Governed by:
Wind direction and speed
Dimensions and slope of the field
Obstacles on final approach path
Proceed directly to the landing area
Goal: Be on downwind, abeam the landing point at normal pattern altitude
If above pattern altitude, circle over the approach end while descending (steep spiral)
Turn in the same direction you intend to fly the pattern
RM: Following or changing the flight path to the landing area 				AI.XII.B.R2
Adjust as conditions change
Best practice is to go directly to the landing area & circle overhead, with a plan to enter the pattern
Divide attention between flying / checklists
Constantly assess the approach
Adjust the pattern based on altitude, wind, etc. to safely reach the landing area 		AI.XII.B.K3
Make the approach as normal as possible
Base & final turns are positioned based on altitude, wind, obstructions, etc.
Strong headwind = closer base Tailwind = farther out base
If high, delay base leg; if low, turn early, or go direct to landing area
If too high, consider:
Extending the pattern
S-turns
Configuring early
Slipping
If too low, consider:
Tightening the pattern
Proceeding directly to the landing area
Delaying configuration
Maintaining best glide
Stable Approach 										AI.XII.B.K4
The more stable the approach, the more predictable the approach
Maintain best glide, and attempt to make the approach as normal as possible
Flying the airplane is the highest priority
Energy Management
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management for more detailed energy management concepts - Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Configuration 											AI.XII.B.R4
Intent is to touchdown in a normal landing configuration (emergency permitting)
Flaps will be gradually lowered based on the conditions, situation, airplane performance, etc.
Have a standard position to lower the flaps and adjust based on the situation
Too high: Configure earlier (or delay configuration and slip, vary the base leg, etc.)
Too low: Delay configuration (tighten the base leg and/or turn to final)
Once flaps are lowered, they should not be retracted
Landing flaps should only be lowered once the landing area is assured
Contacting ATC
If on frequency with ATC, transmit “Mayday, mayday, mayday.” If not on frequency, use guard 121.5
Let them know who you are, where you are, and what you’re doing
The radios will likely be kept on until just before landing. Keep ATC apprised of the situation / plan
If time and conditions permit, squawk emergency - 7700
ATC Emergency Services 									AI.XII.B.K6
Priority: The frequency is basically yours, whatever you need
Aircraft Separation: Any other potentially hazardous aircraft will be moved out of your way
Advice: Nearby airports, etc.
Emergency Response: ATC will coordinate with the tower or local emergency response
Landing
If a restart is not an option, complete the Emergency Landing Checklist
Keep the electrical equipment on as long as practical to make radio calls, use the flaps, etc.
Gear & Flaps
Gear and flaps should only be lowered after landing is assured
Gear can provide better protection in the case of stumps, rocks, or other obstacles
If the field is excessively soft, wet, short, or snow covered, a gear up landing may be safer
If practical, hold the wheels off to allow for a gentle touchdown, like a soft field landing
At this point, the safety of the passengers is the only concern, the airplane does not matter
RM: Descent Factors 										AI.XII.B.R1
Altitude
Dictates the distance the aircraft can travel (use AGL, not MSL)
Know approximate distance traveled at best glide per 1,000’ – apply to the situation
The goal is to put the aircraft at a normal pattern altitude at a normal key position
Wind
During the approach
It can influence glide distance (headwind vs tailwind vs crosswind)
The stronger the wind on final, the closer the base leg needs to be to make a normal approach
Tailwind
A tailwind increases the runway required for landing
Maximum Demonstrated Crosswind Component
If possible, don’t exceed it as the aircraft may not be able to remain with the confines of the runway
Terrain & Obstructions
Be especially cautious of terrain/obstructions during an emergency approach & landing
Without an engine, there may not be enough energy to clear the terrain
Available Landing Distance
Be familiar with the landing distance needed for an emergency approach & pick a suitable landing area
Landing distance at off airport landing areas will have to be estimated from the air
Emergency Locating Devices (ELT)								AI.XII.B.K5
ELT: Small, self-contained transmitter that will automatically, upon impact, transmit an emergency signal
Transmits the emergency signal on 121.5, 243, and/or 406 MHz
Numerous private companies produce emergency locating devices that can be carried on oneself
Basic Personal Locator Beacons (PLBs)
Satellite Messengers
Mental Attitude
The survival records favor pilots who maintain their composure and know how to apply the concepts and procedures developed through the years. Success is as much a matter of the mind as of skills
“We don’t rise to the level of our expectations; we fall to the level of our training”
Common Errors 										AI.XII.B.K7
Improper airspeed control
Poor judgment in the selection of an emergency landing area
Failure to estimate the approximate wind speed and direction
Failure to fly the most suitable pattern for existing situation
Failure to accomplish the emergency checklist
Undershooting or overshooting selected emergency landing area
RM: Hazards
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.XII.B.R5
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Quick, panicked maneuvers can result in a stall or loss of control close to the ground
Especially important in engine failure emergencies
Be aware of, and avoid, obstructions, towers, etc.
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
During engine failures, maintain best glide – Stalls could be catastrophic low/without power
At low level, recover at any indication of a stall then adjust to make the emergency landing
Spin (Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries - follow POH procedures)
A spin is a result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Maintain coordination – don’t cross the controls especially during an emergency landing
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Stop whatever you’re doing and recover at the first sign of a stall
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
Once the spin has stopped, neutralize the rudders and raise the nose - be careful not to stall
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain): AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists & know your aircraft and equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.XII.B.R3
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program)
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
Pertinent to emergencies: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Be cautious, other aircraft may not know you’re in distress
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Research obstacles in the area - Charts, NOTAMs, Terminal procedures, etc.
Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL and support guy wires can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots frequently follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.XII.B.R6
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem and fix it
Especially important to avoid distractions in an emergency with numerous tasks to manage
Situational Awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
High task load during an emergency can lead to a loss of SA
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning - Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Emergency Descent: Maintain SA in relation to the level-off altitude, emergency & associated procedures, airplane configuration, and the plan (diversion)
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention for more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Organization is especially important in situations like this – many tasks, little time
“Attack the closest alligator”
When tasks are piling up, handle the most threatening problem
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: XII.C. System & Equipment Malfunctions
Introduction
How
Note: This lesson provides generic procedures & malfunction discussions – Always follow the POH procedures
Malfunction Procedures (MATL)
Maintain Aircraft Control
Fly the airplane, get to a safe flight state (straight-and-level, etc.)
Trim the aircraft and turn on the autopilot, if possible
Maintaining control continues throughout the malfunction
RM: Undesired aircraft state (UAS) 							AI.XII.C.R4
Some mechanical failures can directly cause departure from normal flight
Ex: Asymmetric flaps, malfunctioning/binding controls, runaway trim
Knowledge of systems & POH procedures helps to minimize a mechanical issue’s impact & prevent upsets
Distractions can lead to, and quickly amplify, the malfunction being dealt with
Maintaining control is the top priority – in the case of an UAS:
Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize
Understand that the specific malfunction may limit or prevent recovery
Further emphasizes the need to maintain control
Analyze the Situation
Indications, lights, sounds, sight (i.e., smoke, leaks, fire, etc.), smells, etc.
Use all available information to determine the issue
Take Proper Action
Apply any memory items
RM: Checklist usage – Use the appropriate checklist from the POH 			AI.XII.C.R2
Land, as conditions require/permit
Based on the emergency, decide on a landing area (divert, field, ditching, etc.)
Power Loss 											AI.XII.C.K1
Rough Running Engine:
Oil Pressure Malfunctions
High Oil Pressure
Possible Cause - Cold oil or possible internal plugging
Corrective Action - If cold, allow the engine to warm, if not, reduce power and land ASAP
Low Oil Pressure
Possible Cause – Broken pressure relief valve, insufficient oil, burned out bearings
Corrective Action – Land as soon as possible
Fluctuating Oil Pressure
Possible Cause – Low oil supply, loose oil lines, defective pressure relief valve
Corrective Action – Land as soon as possible or feather propeller and stop engine (multi-engine)
Engine Overheat
The oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine, and can be caused by blocked lines or empty tanks
In general, turn on boost pumps, switch tanks, verify fuel is on, adjust mixture
Electrical Malfunction 									AI.XII.C.K2a
Electrical Power
Generally, power comes from a generator or alternator
If the generator/alternator fails, typically a battery provides power for a limited amount of time
Battery Time
The higher the amperage load (electrical draw) on the battery, the faster the energy gets consumed
It is very important to shed non-essential loads to provide maximum time
Consumers (see picture for average amperage)
Gear and flaps use significant amounts of power
Procedures
Follow the applicable checklist(s) in the POH
Generic Steps:
Shed all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Notify ATC immediately
Expect a no-flap landing and manual gear extension
Vacuum/Pressure Malfunctions 								AI.XII.C.K2b
What’s Lost?
Heading Indicator & Attitude Indicator
Traditionally, turn coordinators use a different power source than the heading & attitude indicators
Failure results from a loss of the suction or pressure source
As gyros slow, they will begin to wander, displaying incorrect information - Can be slow and insidious
Many small aircraft do not have a warning system for vacuum failure
Look for failure indications – monitor vacuum pressure gauge
Compare the Attitude Indicator with the Turn Coordinator and VSI
Compares static, suction, and electric systems
Identify failed component(s) and use/focus on the functional instruments
Assess the situation - when and where to land may vary based on the conditions and failure(s)
Ex. day VMC versus night over water
Pitot Static Malfunction 									AI.XII.C.K2c
Errors in the ASI/VSI often indicate a pitot and/or static blockage
Blocked Pitot System
Pitot system measures the difference between ram & static pressure
Ram Air Blocked; Drain Hole Open
Air in the system vents through the drain hole, remaining pressure in the pitot tube drops to match the outside (static) pressure
Airspeed decreases to zero
Ram Air and Drain Hole Blocked
Airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter
Ram air pressure in the pitot tube is trapped
Accelerating/decelerating does not affect indications
Static pressure changes with altitude
Blocked Static System
Static system blocked, with pitot tube open
Airspeed
Above the altitude where the port was blocked, airspeed indicates lower than actual
At a lower altitude, airspeed indicates higher than actual
Altimeter freezes at the altitude where the block occurred
Vertical Speed shows a continuous zero indication
Alternate Static Source
Alternate source of static pressure in case the primary is blocked
Normally inside the flight deck
Cabin pressure is lower than exterior pressure
Instrument indications when the alternate static source is used:
Altimeter indicates slightly higher than actual
Airspeed indicates greater than actual
Vertical speed shows a momentary climb and then stabilizes
Electronic Flight Display (EFD) Malfunction 						AI.XII.C.K2d
In an EFD failure, the system reverts to a composite, reversionary mode
Moving map is removed
PFD & engine instruments are combined on the remaining screen
Pilots often become overly reliant on the moving map
Significant loss of SA if the pilot is not prepared for this failure
Stay Prepared
Follow the flight on an enroute chart & have a Chart Supplement on hand
Flap Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2e
Total Flap Failure (no flap approach and landing)
Requires substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
Losing altitude is more difficult so a wider, longer pattern may be necessary
Flown in a relatively nose-high attitude compared to flaps extended
Landing
Airplane is slightly less stable in pitch and roll axes with power reduced and flaps retracted
Tend to float during roundout - Don’t force the plane onto the ground
Don’t flare excessively as it risks a tail strike
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys or retracts while the other remains in position
Indicated by a roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countered with opposite aileron
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher-than-normal airspeed
Hydraulic Malfunction 									AI.XII.C.K2e
If the hydraulic pump were to fail, there are alternate means to raise/lower the gear
Some airplanes will automatically lower the gear
Landing Gear Malfunction 									AI.XII.C.K2e
Alternate gear extension procedure
If this does not solve the problem, a gear up landing is required
Considerations
Airport with crash and rescue facilities
A smooth, hard runway surface tends to cause less damage than a rough, unimproved grass strip
The hard surface creates sparks that could ignite fuel
Burn off excess fuel (if limited to one leg, consume as much fuel from that side as practicable)
Landing the Airplane
One Leg Retracted
Land in a nose-high attitude with wings level
As airspeed slows, apply aileron to keep the unsupported wing airborne as long as possible
After touchdown use full rudder & aggressive braking to maintain some directional control
On a narrow runway, or with ditches/obstacles on the edges, landing with all gear up may be safer
Nose Wheel Retracted
Hold the nose off the ground until almost full-up elevator is applied
Release back pressure to allow the nose to slowly settle to the surface
Do not apply brakes unless necessary to avoid a collision with obstacles
Main Gear Retracted (Nose extended)
Initial contact should be made on the aft fuselage with a nose high attitude
Allow the nose-wheel to gradually touchdown & use nose-wheel steering as necessary
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim 								AI.XII.C.K2f
Grip the controls and maintain control of the plane while disengaging the electric trim system
If the reason for the runaway trim is obvious and has been resolved, re-engage the breaker
Otherwise, leave the system off
Smoke & Fire 											AI.XII.C.K3
In any fire, it is essential the source is discovered first
Identifying the source allows the pilot to fight the fire most effectively
Identify/shutdown the faulty component, extinguish the fire, run the proper checklist, etc.
In-Flight Smoke / Fire
Engine Fire
Usually caused by a failure allowing a combustible substance to contact a hot surface
Indicated by smoke and flames from cowling; and/or discoloration, bubbling, melting of cowling

If the flames are put out, do not attempt to restart the engine
Perform an emergency landing

There may be severe structural damage, and control could be lost at any time
The airplane may still be on fire and susceptible to explosion
The airplane is expendable and the only thing that matters is the safety of those onboard
Electrical Fire
The first indication is usually the distinct odor of burning insulation

If it cannot be detected, the battery master and generator should be turned off
Any materials which have been ignited may continue to burn
If power is essential for the flight, attempt to identify & isolate the faulty circuit:
Electrical master off, then all individual electrical switches off
Electrical master on
Turn on electrical switches one at a time, waiting after each switch to check for signs of fire

Engine Fire/Smoke: Shut down the engine, turn off the electrics and evacuate the airplane
Electrical Fire/Smoke: Immediately turn off the master switch, and shutdown the engine

Do not rush to land – Climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it

Descend and/or use supplemental oxygen (emergency descent)
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression
Other Malfunctions (supplemental oxygen, deicing, etc.) 				AI.XII.C.K4
Reference the POH and/or user’s manual for specific procedures
Common Errors 										AI.XII.C.K6
Inaccurate diagnoses of the malfunction
Use of an improper checklist/procedure
Lack of control throughout the malfunction
Fixation on the malfunction at the expense of the aircraft & safe flight
RM: Hazards
Startle Response 										AI.XII.C.R1
Uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflex, raised heart rate, blood pressure, etc. elicited by exposure to a sudden intense event that violates a pilot’s expectations
Protect against startle response through scenario-based training incorporating realistic distractions
The pilot should react in a calm, controlled manner and use MATL:
Maintain control, Analyze the situation, Take the proper action, Land, as conditions require/permit
Reactions or inputs outside of checklists may aggravate the situation
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.XII.C.R3
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem and fix it
Especially important to avoid distractions in an emergency with numerous tasks to manage
Situational Awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
High task load during an emergency can lead to a loss of SA
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning - Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Emergency Descent: Maintain SA in relation to the level-off altitude, emergency & associated procedures, airplane configuration, and the plan (diversion)
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention for more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Organization is especially important in situations like this – many tasks, little time
“Attack the closest alligator”
When tasks are piling up, handle the most threatening problem
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

Apply any memory items

Pitot system measures the difference between ram & static pressure

Air in the system vents through the drain hole, remaining pressure in the pitot tube drops to match the outside (static) pressure
Airspeed decreases to zero

Airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter
Ram air pressure in the pitot tube is trapped
Accelerating/decelerating does not affect indications
Static pressure changes with altitude

Static system blocked, with pitot tube open
Airspeed
Above the altitude where the port was blocked, airspeed indicates lower than actual
At a lower altitude, airspeed indicates higher than actual
Altimeter freezes at the altitude where the block occurred
Vertical Speed shows a continuous zero indication

paragraphs.text: XII.D. Emergency Equipment & Survival Gear
Introduction
How
Appropriate Equipment 									AI.XII.D.K3
For flight over uninhabited areas, it’s wise to have/understand proper survival equipment for the climate/terrain
General plan is equipment and gear for 48-72 hours, adjust as required
A survival kit should provide sustenance, shelter, medical care, and a means to summon help
Consider the terrain, the climate/season, and type of emergency communication equipment needed
General items to consider
Think outside the box
What parts of the airplane/baggage could be used for survival?
Ex: The aircraft cover could be used for shelter, warmth, etc.
More specific items should be considered based on the type of terrain and wildlife
Climate Extremes 									AI.XII.D.K3a
Cold
Warm clothes and layers, gloves, headgear, boots, snowshoes
Waterproof layer(s)
Blanket(s)
Shovel
Hand/body warmers
Hot
Light clothing & hat (sun protection), sunglasses, sunscreen, extra water
Mountainous Terrain 									AI.XII.D.K3b
Mosquito head net
Hiking boots
Warm/Cold weather clothing to adapt to temperature changes
Bear spray, or similar items depending on the wildlife
Overwater 										AI.XII.D.K3c
Life vests, Dry suit/survival suit
Raft
Equipment Use & Care
Onboard emergency equipment often consists of an ELT, fire extinguisher, emergency axe, & your survival gear
ELT 												AI.XII.D.K1
Purpose – Transmit a downed aircraft’s location for search and rescue personnel
Broadcasts on 121.5 and 243.0 (no longer monitored by satellite), and 406 MHz
Operation/Use – Emits a signal for rescue crews. Designed to automatically activate in a crash
Operates continuously for at least 48 hours over a wide temperature range
Know how to activate the ELT and ensure transmitting
Servicing – Must be checked every 12 calendar months
FAR 91.207: The battery must be replaced after 1-hour cumulative use or ½ its useful life
ELT Testing
Analog 121.5/243 MHz ELTs – Test only during the first 5 minutes after any hour
Digital 406 MHz ELTs – Test in accordance with the unit's manufacturer's instructions
Airborne tests are not permitted
Storage – Usually installed by the manufacturer to prevent damage to the device in a crash
Fire Extinguisher 										AI.XII.D.K2
Purpose - Used to fight/extinguish fires (check the types of fires it’s intended to fight)
Operation – Generally, pull the pin, point, and squeeze the handle (verify operating instructions)
Aim at the base of the fire
Servicing – Verify the extinguisher isn’t expired, has been inspected, and contains the proper charge
Storage – Ensure it is attached where it is supposed to be, securely in its mount
Emergency Axe
Purpose – To provide a means to exit in case the doors cannot be opened
Operation – If door(s) can’t be opened, use the axe to escape as described by the manufacturer
Servicing – Ensure the axe is onboard and properly mounted, and inspected as required
Storage – The axe should be stored in its mount as the manufacturer intends
RM: Survival Gear (for 48-72 hours) 								AI.XII.D.R1
Purpose – Used for survival (food, water, shelter, warmth, etc.)
Operation/Use – The operation / use will vary with equipment. Use based on the instructions
Servicing – Verify the equipment is in good working order & doesn’t need to be replaced, cleaned, etc.
Ensure electronic equipment is in good working order and properly charged/ for use
Adjust the contents of the survival gear based on the trip, weather, terrain, etc.
Storage – Store the gear safely and accessibly on the airplane
Ballistic Parachute 										AI.XII.D.K4
Acts as an alternative to certain emergency situations
Parachute deploys from the plane allowing a slow descent & occupants to survive with minimal injury
Understand and follow procedures for arming/disarming and conditions under which it should be used
Conditions for Deployment
Examples include catastrophic loss of controllability, pilot incapacitation, and loss of control
Airframe will be lost, but if deployed in an acceptable flight regime it can prevent injuries & save lives
Passenger Brief
RM: Conditions for a Safe Deployment 							AI.XII.D.R2
When & How to deploy it
What to expect
Applicable hazards (Ex. Ground hazards with a deployed parachute, surface winds)
Evacuation procedures once on the ground
Instructor ACS Appendix 3 XII.D.
Follow the manufacturer’s procedures for arming/disarming the system before and after flight
Knowledge testing may include simulation and briefing of procedures but not actual deployment
Emergency Autoland (EAL) Systems 							AI.XII.D.K5
Designed to be deployed in the case of pilot incapacitation
How it Works
Manually activated by a pilot or passenger
Automatic Activation
If the system sense erratic flying, it stabilizes the aircraft, and checks for pilot responsiveness
Without further input, it initiates an emergency descent
If there is no further input, it initiates the process for an automated landing
Transmits automated messages on the last selected frequency and Guard & squawks 7700
Call sign and intention to divert to a particular airport and runway
Passenger Brief
RM: Conditions for a safe deployment 							AI.XII.D.R3
When & How to deploy it
What to expect
Evacuation procedures on the ground
Any applicable hazards
FAA Safety Team Emergency Autoland Overview
Common Errors 										AI.XII.D.K6
Failure to carry appropriate gear and equipment for the route
Failure to maintain the equipment/gear
Lack of understanding of the operation and use of emergency gear & equipment
Failure to understand when and how to deploy emergency systems (i.e., parachute & Autoland)
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: XII.C. Systems and Equipment Malfunctions
Select the aircraft Systems and Equipment Malfunctions lesson from the Navigation Pane, or use the links below:
GENERIC
Generic Aircraft Malfunctions
CESSNA
Cessna 152
Cessna 172S G1000
CIRRUS
Cirrus SR20
DIAMOND
Diamond DA20
Diamond DA40
PIPER
Piper Archer II (PA-28-181)
Piper Archer III (PA-28-181)
Piper Arrow (PA-28R-201)
XII.C. Generic
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story

Wouldn’t it be fun to be flying one day and experience a problem that you have no idea how to deal with? Of course not, that’s why it’s important to understand your equipment and the proper procedures associated.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Systems and equipment malfunctions involve the knowledge and procedures to handle problems that may occur in the airplane.
Why

The key to successful management of an emergency, and/or preventing a non-normal situation from progressing into a true emergency, is a thorough knowledge of, and adherence to, the necessary procedures.
How:
Note: This lesson provides generic procedures & malfunction discussions. Always follow the POH procedures.
Malfunction Procedures (MATL)
Maintain Aircraft Control
Fly the airplane
Get to a safe flight state (straight-and-level, etc.)
Trim the aircraft and turn on the autopilot, if possible
Maintaining control continues throughout the malfunction
Do not let the issue, checklists, etc. distract from flying the airplane
Divide attention between flying and checklists/procedures
RM: Distractions can lead to an undesired aircraft state (UAS) 				AI.XII.C.R4
Can quickly amplify the malfunction already being dealt with
The malfunction could also be the reason for the UAS
Maintaining control is the top priority – in the case of an UAS:
Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize as required
Understand the specific malfunction may limit or prevent recovery
Further emphasizes the need to maintain control
Analyze the Situation
Indications, lights, sounds, visual (i.e., smoke, leaks, fire, etc.), smells, etc.
Use all available information to determine the issue
Take the Proper Action
Apply any memory items
RM: Checklist usage – Use the appropriate checklist from the POH 				AI.XII.C.R2
Checklist is the safest, most effective way to handle the problem
Don’t go rogue and make up your own procedure/guess
Potential to not fix the problem and/or cause other problems
Land, as conditions require/permit
Based on the emergency, decide on a landing area (divert, field, ditching, etc.)
This may have to occur in conjunction with the checklist(s)
Power Loss 												AI.XII.C.K1
Rough running engine:
Oil Pressure Malfunctions
High Oil Pressure
Possible Cause - Cold oil or possible internal plugging
Corrective Action - If cold, allow the engine to warm, if not, reduce power and land ASAP
Low Oil Pressure
Possible Cause – Broken pressure relief valve, insufficient oil, burned out bearings
Corrective Action – Land as soon as possible or feather the propeller and stop the engine (multi-engine)
Fluctuating Oil Pressure
Possible Cause – Low oil supply, loose oil lines, defective pressure relief valve
Corrective Action – Land as soon as possible or feather propeller and stop engine (multi-engine)
Engine Overheat
The oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine, and can be caused by blocked lines or empty tanks
In general, turn on boost pumps, switch tanks, verify fuel is on, adjust mixture
Electrical Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2a
Electrical Power
Generally, power comes from a generator or alternator
If the generator/alternator fails, typically a battery provides power for a limited amount of time
Battery Time
The higher the amperage load (electrical draw) on the battery, the faster the energy gets consumed
Ex: 25-amp hour battery can produce 5 amps per hour for 5 hours
Increasing to 10 amps, it may only last 2 hours
40 amps may discharge the battery in 10-15 mins
Battery condition matters
Over time, power is reduced due to internal resistance
Very important to shed non-essential loads to provide maximum time
Consumers
See picture to right for average amperage
Gear and flaps use significant amounts of power
Using them may result in a total loss of power
Procedures
Follow the applicable checklist(s) in the POH
Reduce electrical load
Fly on the backup instruments
Generic Steps
Shed all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Can vary based on the situation (day/night, VMC/IMC)
Notify ATC immediately – Request vectors for landing at the nearest suitable airport
Expect a no-flap landing and manual gear extension
Vacuum/Pressure Malfunctions 									AI.XII.C.K2b
What’s Lost?
Heading Indicator, Attitude Indicator, and/or Turn Coordinator
Traditionally, turn coordinators use a different power source than the heading / attitude indicators
Ex. Vacuum for the attitude and heading gyros, and electric for the turn coordinator
If the heading & attitude indicators fail, the turn coordinator is still usable, and vice versa
Failure results from a loss of the suction or pressure source (vacuum failure)
As the gyroscopes slow down, they will begin to wander, displaying incorrect information
Can be slow and insidious
Many small aircraft do not have a warning system for vacuum failure
Look for vacuum failure indications – monitor the vacuum pressure gauge
Compare the Attitude Indicator with the Turn Coordinator and VSI
Along with providing pitch / bank information, this compares the static, suction, and electric systems
Identify the failed component(s) and use the remaining functional instruments to maintain control
Assess the situation - when and where to land may vary based on the conditions and failure(s)
Day VMC with backup instruments may allow the pilot to return to their home field
Night, reduced visibility, or minimal horizon may require an emergency and landing at the closest field
Pitot Static Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2c
General
Errors in the ASI and VSI almost always indicate a pitot blockage, static blockage, or both
Moisture, ice, dirt, insects, etc. can cause a blockages
Always preflight the pitot tube and static ports
Blocked Pitot System
Pitot system measures the difference between ram air pressure in the pitot tube and static air pressure from the static port
Static pressure is vented to instrument casing
Ram air is connected to a diaphragm in the case
Ram air blocked, with drain hole open
Air already in the system vents through the drain hole and remaining pressure in the pitot tube drops to match the outside (static) air pressure
Airspeed decreases to zero as ram air pressure and static pressure become equal
Not an instantaneous drop, but happens quickly
Ram air blocked, and drain hole blocked
Big Picture
Airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter
Ram air pressure in the pitot tube is trapped
Accelerating/decelerating does not affect indications
Static pressure changes with altitude
In a climb
Ram air pressure remains constant
Static pressure decreases
Diaphragm expands, just like would happen with an increase in ram air pressure/acceleration
Airspeed increases as altitude increases
In a descent
Ram air pressure remains constant
Static pressure increases
Diaphragm contracts, just like would happen with a decrease in ram air pressure/deceleration
Airspeed decreases as altitude decreases
Airspeed acts like an altimeter, increasing in a climb and decreasing in a descent
Blocked Static System
Static system blocked, with pitot tube open
Airspeed operates but is inaccurate
When above the altitude where the static port(s) were blocked, airspeed indicates lower than actual
Trapped pressure is higher than normal for the altitude
When at a lower altitude, airspeed indicates higher than actual
Trapped pressure is lower than normal for that altitude
Altimeter freezes at the altitude where the block occurred
Vertical Speed shows a continuous zero indication
Alternate Static Source
Provides alternate source of static pressure in the case the primary becomes blocked
Normally inside the flight deck
Cabin pressure is lower than exterior pressure due to venturi effect of air flowing around the fuselage
Instrument indications when the alternate static source is used:
Altimeter indicates slightly higher than actual
Airspeed indicates greater than actual
Vertical speed shows a momentary climb and then stabilizes if altitude is constant
Electronic Flight Display (EFD) Malfunction 								AI.XII.C.K2d
In the case of an EFD failure, the system reverts to a composite, reversionary mode
Moving map is eliminated
PFD and engine instruments are combined on the remaining screen
Pilots often become overly reliant on the moving map
What should be a supplementary source of data becomes a primary navigation tool
Significant loss of situational awareness if the pilot is not prepared for this failure
Stay Prepared
Follow the flight on an enroute chart while monitoring the moving map
Have a Chart Supplement to prevent losing access to airport information
Flap Malfunction 											AI.XII.C.K2e
Total Flap Failure (no flap approach and landing)
Requires substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
Losing altitude is more difficult so a wider, longer pattern may be necessary
Flown in a relatively nose-high attitude compared to flaps extended
On final, this can make it difficult to see the runway
Can lead to errors in judgement of height/distance and cause the perception the plane is close to a stall
Landing
Airplane is slightly less stable in pitch and roll axes with power reduced and flaps retracted
Tend to float during roundout
Don’t force the plane onto the ground
Don’t flare excessively as it risks a tail strike
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys or retracts while the other remains in position
Indicated by a roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countered with opposite aileron
Yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side requires opposite rudder
Almost full aileron may be necessary at reduced airspeeds to maintain wings level
Do not attempt to land with a cross-wind from the side of the deployed flap
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
The wing with the retracted flap will stall earlier - possible cross-controlled stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher-than-normal airspeed
Hydraulic Malfunction  										AI.XII.C.K2e
If the hydraulic pump were to fail, there are alternate means to raise/lower the gear
Some airplanes will automatically lower the gear
Landing Gear Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2e
Alternate gear extension procedure
If this does not solve the problem, a gear up landing is required
Considerations
Airport with crash and rescue facilities
A smooth, hard runway surface tends to cause less damage than a rough, unimproved grass strip
The hard surface does create sparks that could ignite fuel
Can request for the runway to be foamed, if available
Burn off excess fuel
Reduced landing speed and chance of fire
If the malfunction is limited to one leg, consume as much fuel from that side as practicable
Reduced weight on that side allows you to delay contact with the surface until the last moment
Reduced impact speed = reduced damage
Landing the Airplane
One Leg Retracted
Land in a nose-high attitude with wings level
As airspeed slows, apply aileron to keep the unsupported wing airborne as long as possible
After touchdown, the airplane will veer strongly in the direction of the faulty gear leg/dragging wing
Use full opposite rudder and aggressive braking to maintain some degree of directional control
On a narrow runway, or one with ditches/obstacles on the edges, landing with all gear up may be safer
Nose Wheel Retracted
Hold the nose off the ground until almost full-up elevator is applied
Release back pressure to allow the nose to slowly settle to the surface
Applying full back pressure results in the nose abruptly dropping to the surface
Can result in burrowing and/or additional damage
Try to gently set the nose on the ground
Do not apply brakes unless necessary to avoid a collision with obstacles
Main Gear Retracted (Nose extended)
Initial contact should be made on the aft fuselage with a nose high attitude
Helps to prevent porpoising and/or wheelbarrowing
Allow the nose-wheel to gradually touchdown
Use nose-wheel steering as necessary
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim 									AI.XII.C.K2f
Grip the controls and maintain control of the plane while disengaging the electric trim system
Disengage button, circuit breaker, etc.
If the reason for the runaway trim is obvious and has been resolved, engage the breaker
Smoke & Fire  											AI.XII.C.K3
In any fire, it is essential the source is discovered first
Identifying the source allows the pilot to fight the fire most effectively
Identify/shutdown the faulty component, use the extinguisher effectively, run the proper checklist, etc.
In-Flight Smoke/Fire
Engine Fire
Usually caused by a failure allowing a combustible substance to contact a hot surface
Indicated by smoke / flames from cowling; and / or discoloration, bubbling, melting of cowling
Unless the POH says otherwise, 1st step should be to shut off fuel
If the flames are put out, do not attempt to restart the engine
Perform an emergency landing
Keep in mind:
There may be severe structural damage and control could be lost at any time
Airplane may still be on fire and susceptible to explosion
Airplane is expendable and the only thing that matters is the safety of those onboard
Electrical Fires
First indication is usually the distinct odor of burning insulation
Try to identify the problem by checking circuit breakers, lights, instruments, avionics
If it cannot be detected, the battery master and generator should be turned off
Any materials which have been ignited may continue to burn
If power is essential for the flight, attempt to identify / isolate the faulty circuit:
Electrical master off, then all individual electrical switches off
Electrical master on
Turn on electrical switches one at a time, waiting after each switch to check for signs of fire
Turn off / do not use any equipment that restarts the fire. Other equipment can be used
Cabin Fires
Usually result from smoking, electrical system malfunctions, and heating system malfunctions
Two immediate demands:
Attacking the fire, and getting the airplane safely on the ground as quickly as possible
In general, identify and shutdown the cause of the fire
Smoke can often be cleared by opening air vents – only after using the fire extinguisher
If smoke increases, immediately close them
Windows can also be used to help clear smoke
Use oxygen if the smoke is severe; initiate an immediate descent
Ground Smoke / Fire

Do not rush to land (climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing)
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it

Common Errors 											AI.XII.C.K6
Inaccurate diagnoses of the malfunction
Use of an improper checklist/procedure
Lack of control throughout the malfunction
Fixation on the malfunction at the expense of the aircraft & safe flight
RM: Hazards
Startle Response										AI.XII.C.R1
Uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflex, raised heart rate, blood pressure, etc. elicited by exposure to a sudden intense event that violates a pilot’s expectations
Protect against startle response through scenario-based training incorporating realistic distractions
The pilot should react in a calm, controlled manner and:
Maintain aircraft control
Analyze the situation
Take the proper action
Land, as conditions require/permit
Reactions or inputs outside of checklists may likely aggravate the situation

Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem and fix it
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Especially important to avoid distractions in an emergency with numerous tasks to manage
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
High task load during an emergency can lead to a loss of SA
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition

Divide attention between the aircraft & malfunction, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention for more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Organization is especially important in situations like this – many tasks, little time
“Attack the closest alligator”
When tasks are piling up, handle the most threatening problem
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate

Brief review of the main points
Understanding different emergencies and how to deal with them is obviously important as you will always be prepared and be able to react quickly in the event one of these emergencies occurs.

Electrical system malfunctions
Heating system malfunctions

Rough Running Engine or Partial Power Loss
Checklist
Loss of Engine Oil Pressure
High Oil Pressure
Possible Cause - Cold oil or possible internal plugging
Corrective Action - If cold, allow the engine to warm, if not, reduce power and land ASAP
Low Oil Pressure
Possible Cause - Broken Pressure Relief Valve, Insufficient Oil, Burned Out Bearings
Corrective Action - Land ASAP or feather the prop and stop engine
Checklist
Oil Temp: CHECK
If Pressure drops below Green Arc but Temp is normal: LAND AT NEAREST FIELD
If Pressure drops below Green Arc and Temp is rising: REDUCE THROTTLE TO MIN REQ POWER
Be prepared for engine failure and emergency landing
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine, and can be caused by blocked lines or empty tanks

Fuel Shutoff: OPEN
Mixture: FULL RICH
Electric Fuel Pump: ON

Engine Overheat
The oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Causes and Corrective Action
Hydraulic Malfunction (not applicable to DA20)
If the hydraulic pump were to fail, there are manual means to raise/lower the gear
Some airplanes will automatically lower the gear (DA42)
Electrical Malfunction
The generator/alternator is the cause of most electrical system failures (indicated on the ammeter)
Once the generator goes offline, the only electrical source remaining is the battery
The battery although may have very little time available
Electrically powered gear and flaps use up power at rates much greater than most other equipment
Selecting these motors on a partially depleted battery could result in immediate loss of power
Steps
Turn off all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Save as much power as possible
Notify ATC immediately and request vectors for a landing at the nearest airport
Expect to make a no flap landing, and anticipate a manual gear extension
Checklist
Total Electrical Failure
Generator Failure (GEN. Annunciator Light Illuminated)
GEN/BAT Master: Cycle Generator Master Switch OFF - ON
Generator Circuit Breaker: RESET, if tripped
Generator Control Breaker: RESET, if tripped
If GEN cannot be brought online: Switch off all non-flight essential electrical consumers
Monitor the Ammeter and Voltmeter
Land at the nearest airport
Low Voltage Indication (Needle in yellow arc) While on the Ground

Non-Flight Essential Electrical Consumers: OFF
If needle stays in the yellow arc, and the ammeter indicates a discharge, use GEN FAILURE
Induction Icing
As air is ingested through the engine intakes, the moisture can freeze inside the induction system, reducing or stopping the flow of combustible air to the engine
Ice can also form on the exterior of the airplane, and clog the air intake openings
Corrective Action
Use the Alternate Air source
Icing Checklist
Leave icing area (change altitude or flight direction to reach a higher temp)
Continue to move the control surfaces to maintain mobility
Alternate Air: ON
Increase RPM to avoid icing of prop blades
Cabin Heat: ON DEFROST
Door or Window Opening in Flight
In the event of an inadvertent door opening in flight or on takeoff, adhere to the following:
Concentrate on flying the plane, an open door seldom compromises the ability of the plane to fly
Do not rush to land the plane if the door opens during lift off
Climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it
Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then settle partially closed
A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim
Checklist
Control Stick: Grip stick and maintain control of the airplane
Trim Motor Circuit Breaker: PULL the breaker
Rocker Switch: Check if depressed
If the reason for the runaway trim is obvious and has been resolved, engage the breaker
Flap Malfunction
Total Flap Failure
This will necessitate a no flap approach and landing
This will require substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
The airplane must be flown in a relatively nose-high attitude as compared to flaps extended
This can make the runway difficult to see
A wider, longer pattern may be necessary to avoid diving to lose altitude and building up airspeed
The airplane will tend to float considerably during roundout
If only flaps are unavailable, raise the approach airspeed 10 knots and maintain a flat approach angle
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys/retracts while the other remains in position
The problem is indicated by a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countering
Countered with opposite aileron
The yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side will require opposite rudder
Aileron and opposite rudder results in a cross controlled situation
Almost full aileron may be necessary at the reduced airspeed to maintain wings level
Therefore, do not attempt to land with a cross-wind from the side of the deployed flap
The additional roll control to counteract the cross-wind may not be available
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
The wing with the retracted flap will stall much earlier - possible cross-controlled stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher than normal airspeed
Pressurization Malfunction
Descend or use supplemental oxygen
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression

Brief review of the main points

Carburetor Icing
A gradual loss of RPM and eventual engine roughness may result from the formation of carburetor ice
To clear the ice:
Apply full throttle
Pull the carb heat knob full out until the engine runs smoothly
Remove the carb heat and readjust the throttle
If conditions require continued use of carb heat in flight, use the minimum amount of heat necessary to prevent ice from forming and lean the mixture slightly for smoothest engine operation
Spark Plug Fouling
Slight engine roughness can be caused by spark plug fouling (carbon or lead deposit on the spark plug)
Verify by turning the mags switch momentarily from Both to either L or R. An obvious power loss in single mag operation is evidence of spark plug or magneto trouble
Procedure (assuming spark plugs are the issue. Magento malfunction is described below)
Lean the mixture to the recommended lean setting for cruise flight

If the problem does not clear up in several minutes, determine if a richer mixture setting will produce smoother operation. If not, proceed to the nearest airport for repairs using the Both position of the mags switch unless extreme roughness makes a single mag position necessary
Magneto Malfunction
Sudden engine roughness or misfiring is usually a sign of a magneto problem
Changing the mags from Both to L and R positions will identify the malfunctioning magneto
Procedure

Select different power settings and enrichen the mixture to determine if continued operation on Both mags is practicable. If not, change to the good mag and continue to the nearest airport for repairs

Hydraulic Malfunction
Brake failure
Symptoms of impending brake failure:
Gradual decrease in braking action after brake application
Noisy or dragging brakes
Soft or spongy pedals
Excessive brake travel
Weak braking action

Electrical Malfunction
General
The generator/alternator is the cause of most electrical system failures
Once the generator goes offline, the only electrical source remaining is the battery
The battery although may have very little time available
Electrically powered gear and flaps use up power at rates much greater than most other equipment
Selecting these motors on a partially depleted battery could result in immediate loss of power
Malfunctions in the electrical system can be detected through regular monitoring of the ammeter and low-voltage warning light
The cause of these malfunctions is usually difficult to determine
A broken alternator drive belt or wiring is the most likely cause of alternator failures
A damaged or improperly adjusted alternator control unit can also cause malfunctions
Electrical power malfunctions generally fall into two categories:
Excessive Rate of Charge

After 30 minutes of cruise flight, the main battery ammeter should be indicating less than 2 needle widths of charging current. If the charging current remains above this value on a long flight, the battery electrolyte could overheat and evaporate
Electronic components can be adversely affected by higher than normal voltage
The Alternator Control Unit should disconnect the alternator if the charge increases to more than 31.5 volts

If the ACU does not operate correctly, the alternator should be turned off, alternator circuit breaker pulled, nonessential electrical equipment turned off, and the flight terminated as soon as practical
Insufficient Rate of Charge
i.e. the alternator is not providing the necessary charge
If the over-voltage sensor shuts down the alternator, or the alternator circuit breaker trips a discharge will be show on the ammeter followed by the low-voltage warning light
This may be a nuisance trip, attempt to energize the alternator system by:
Turning off the radios
Checking the alternator circuit breaker is in
Turning the master switch off and back on
If this doesn’t reset the system, there is an alternator system problem
The flight should be terminated and the current drain on the battery minimized to extend the amount of time on battery power
If the emergency occurs at night, power must be conserved for later use of the landing light and flaps

Turn off all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Save as much power as possible
Notify ATC immediately and request vectors for a landing at the nearest airport
Expect to make a no flap landing, and anticipate a manual gear extension
