Malfunctions in the electrical system can be detected through regular monitoring of the main battery ammeter (M Batt Amps) and the main electric bus voltmeter (M Bus Volts)
Electrical power malfunctions generally fall into two categories:
Excessive Rate of Charge

After 30 minutes of flight, the main battery ammeter should be indicating less than 5 amps. If the charging current remains above this value on a long flight, the battery electrolyte could overheat and evaporate
Electronic components can be adversely affected by higher than normal voltage
The Alternator Control Unit should disconnect the alternator if the charge increases to more than 31.75 volts
If the ACU does not operate correctly, the Master Switch (Alt only) should be turned Off
Insufficient Rate of Charge
i.e. the alternator is not providing the necessary charge
The ACU can de-energize the alternator due to a minor disturbance in the electrical system, resulting in a nuisance opening of the Alt Field circuit breaker
Attempt to energize the alternator system by turning the Master Switch (Alt) Off, check the Alt Field circuit breaker is in and then turning the Master Switch (Alt) back on
If this doesn’t reset the system, there is an alternator system problem (more below)
General Steps to any electrical malfunction
Turn off all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Save as much power as possible
Notify ATC immediately and request vectors for a landing at the nearest airport
Expect to make a no flap landing, and anticipate a manual gear extension

Induction Icing
POH Amplified Emergency Procedures
Flight into icing conditions is prohibited and extremely dangerous
The best action is to turn back or change altitude to escape the icing conditions

As air is ingested through the engine intakes, the moisture can freeze inside the induction system, reducing or stopping the flow of combustible air to the engine. In extremely rare instances, ice can completely block the fuel injection air reference tubes
Ice can also form on the exterior of the airplane, and clog the air intake openings

In all situations mentioned, the throttle should be positioned for maximum RPM (in some instances, the throttle may need to be retarded to obtain maximum RPM). The mixture should then be adjusted for maximum RPM
Corrective Action
Use the Alternate Air source

Door or Window Opening in Flight
In the event of an inadvertent door opening in flight or on takeoff, adhere to the following:
Concentrate on flying the plane, an open door seldom compromises the ability of the plane to fly
Do not rush to land the plane if the door opens during lift off
Climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it
Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then settle partially closed
A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed

Checklist

Total Flap Failure
This will necessitate a no flap approach and landing
This will require substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more depending on the aircraft – reference the POH performance)
The airplane must be flown in a relatively nose-high attitude as compared to flaps extended
This can make the runway difficult to see
A wider, longer pattern may be necessary to avoid diving to lose altitude and building up airspeed
The airplane will tend to float considerably during roundout
If only flaps are unavailable, raise the approach airspeed 10 knots and maintain a flat approach angle
This is a general recommendation and not from the Cessna 172 POH
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys/retracts while the other remains in position
The problem is indicated by a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countering
Countered with opposite aileron
The yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side will require opposite rudder
Aileron and opposite rudder results in a crossed control situation
Almost full aileron may be necessary at the reduced airspeed to maintain wings level
Therefore, do not attempt to land with a cross-wind from the side of the deployed flap
The additional roll control to counteract the cross-wind may not be available
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
The wing with the retracted flap will stall much earlier - possible crossed control stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher than normal airspeed
Pressurization Malfunction
Descend or use supplemental oxygen
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression

Engine Partial Power Loss – Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH
Indications

Selecting the other fuel tank may fix the problem if fuel starvation or contamination is the issue

Intake icing may lead to engine roughness – Opening the alternate air may fix the problem

If you can safely maintain level flight, land at a suitable airfield as soon as conditions permit

Flight Operations
General

The source of the fire must be promptly identified. Check for the source of the fire first
Identifiers like instrument readings, characters of the smoke (smell, color, location), etc.
Electrical Fire in Flight
Engine Fire in Flight
Rough Running Engine or Partial Power Loss
General
Engine roughness is usually due to carburetor icing which is indicated by a drop in RPM, and may be accompanied by a slight loss of airspeed or altitude
If too much ice is allowed to accumulate, restoration of full power may not be possible; therefore, prompt action is required
Procedure
Loss of Engine Oil Pressure
General
Can be a partial or total loss of oil pressure
Partial Loss
Usually indicates a malfunction in the oil pressure regulating system, and a landing should be made as soon as possible to investigate the cause and prevent engine damage
Complete Loss
May signify oil exhaustion or may be the result of a faulty gauge
In either case, proceed toward the nearest airport and be prepared for a forced landing. If the problem is not a pressure gauge malfunction, the engine may stop suddenly
Maintain altitude until such time as a dead stick landing can be accomplished
Don’t change power settings unnecessarily, this may hasten complete power loss

Depending on the circumstances, it may be advisable to make an off airport landing while power is still available, particularly if other indication of actual oil pressure loss, such as sudden increases in temperatures, or oil smoke, are apparent, and an airport is not close
Procedures
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine, and can be caused by blocked fuel lines or empty tanks
Unless recognized immediately, the most likely course of action is to run the Engine Roughness checklist, or Engine Power Loss in Flight checklist
In the case of fuel starvation, a power off landing will be necessary using the Power Off Landing checklist
Plan ahead while on the ground, and monitor fuel while in flight to prevent fuel starvation
If at any point during flight the fuel required is not in line with the fuel available create a new plan. Divert immediately if necessary, don’t rely on hope!
Engine Overheat
General
The oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Watch the oil pressure gauge for an accompanying loss of pressure
A steady rise in oil temperature is a sign of trouble. Land at the nearest airport and let a mechanic investigate the problem
Rising oil temperature may be the result of a low oil level, and obstruction in the oil cooler, damaged or improper baffle seals, a defective gauge, or other causes
High Oil Temperature Procedures
Land at the nearest airport and investigate the problem
Prepare for power off landing

XII.C. Piper Archer III (PA-28-181)
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story

Wouldn’t it be fun to be flying one day and experience a problem that you have no idea how to deal with? Of course not, that’s why it’s important to understand your equipment and the proper procedures associated.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Systems and equipment malfunctions involve knowing how to handle problems that may occur in the airplane to provide as safe a flight as possible.
Why

The key to successful management of an emergency situation, and/or preventing a non-normal situation from progressing into a true emergency, is a thorough knowledge of, and adherence to, the necessary procedures.
How:
General Info
Review 3.1 General in the POH
CAS Messages
PFD Annunciations & Alerts
Aural Alerts
Terminology (Land as soon as practical vs possible)
Review 3.3 Airspeeds for Safe Operation
Smoke, Fire, or Both, During Ground or Flight Operations
Ground Operations
Engine Fire During Start - Usually the result of overpriming
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Intent is to draw the fire back into the engine
Flight Operations
General
Presence of fire is noted through smoke, smell, and/or heat in the cabin
Essential that the source of the fire be promptly identified
Identifiers like instrument readings, characters of the smoke (smell, color, location), etc.
Pilot judgement and a thorough understanding of the systems is critical
Engine Fire in Flight
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Electrical Fire in Flight
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Rough Running Engine or Partial Power Loss
General Considerations
Engine Roughness – Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
May be caused by blockage in the injector nozzles, induction system icing, or ignition problems
Follow the procedures, check the gauges for abnormal readings and proceed accordingly
Engine Power Loss in Flight – Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Complete power loss is usually caused by fuel interruption
Loss of Engine Oil Pressure
Checklist Information
Can be a partial or total loss of oil pressure
Partial Loss
Usually indicates a malfunction in the oil pressure regulating system,
Landing should be made as soon as possible to investigate the cause and prevent damage
Complete Loss
May signify oil exhaustion or may be the result of a faulty gauge
In either case, proceed toward the nearest airport and be prepared for a forced landing
If the problem is not a pressure gauge malfunction, the engine may stop suddenly
Maintain altitude until such time as a dead stick landing can be accomplished
Don’t change power settings unnecessarily, this may hasten complete power loss
Oil Pressure Checklist – Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine
Unless recognized, likely to run Engine Roughness checklist, or Engine Power Loss in Flight checklist
Engine Power Loss In Flight – Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Complete power loss is usually caused by fuel flow interruption
Water in the fuel may take time to clear – allowing the prop to windmill may restore power
If the selected tank is empty, it can take up to 10 seconds after switching tanks to restart
Engine Roughness – Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
May be caused by blockage in the injector nozzles
Adjusting mixture, turning on electric fuel pump & swapping tanks may help with fuel issues
If power is not regained, a power off landing will be necessary using the Power Off Landing checklist
Plan ahead while on the ground and monitor fuel while in flight to prevent fuel starvation
If at any point the fuel remaining does not reasonably resemble the plan, assess the situation
If necessary, divert immediately – don’t rely on hope!
Engine Overheat
General
Oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Watch the oil pressure gauge for an accompanying loss of pressure
General Causes and Corrective Action
Oil Temperature – Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Causes: Low oil level, oil cooler obstruction, damager or improper baffle seals, faulty indication, etc.
Land as soon as possible and have the cause investigated
Hydraulic Malfunction
General Brake Failure Procedures – Not in the POH
Symptoms of impending brake failure:
Gradual decrease in braking action after brake application
Noisy or dragging brakes
Soft or spongy pedals
Excessive brake travel
Weak braking action
If braking action decreases, let up on the pedals and the reapply with heavy pressure
If the brakes become spongy or pedal travel increases, pumping the pedals should build pressure
If one brake is weak or fails, use the other sparingly with opposite rudder to offset the good brake
If both brakes have failed, select the longest landing surface available
Make a controlled landing w/o excessive float – slow straight ahead with aerodynamic braking
Electrical Malfunction
Alternator Failure
If a momentary overvoltage caused the failure, resetting the ALTR switch should fix the problem
If the alternator does not reset, the battery is the primary source of power
Essential Bus is only bus powered
When the battery dies, the emergency battery should automatically activate
If it doesn’t turn off BATT MASTR and ALTR switches
About 30 mins of power
Alternator Failure – Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Complete Electrical Failure
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Inoperative Equipment while on Emergency Bus
PFD, Engine instruments (except oil pressure), Com / Nav 1, Standby instrument, Audio panel, Avionics lighting/dimming
Emergency Battery Voltage
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Complete electrical failure is imminent – Land as soon as possible
Induction Icing
General
As air is ingested through the engine intakes, the moisture can freeze inside the induction system, reducing or stopping the flow of combustible air to the engine
Ice can also form on the exterior of the airplane, and clog the air intake openings
Induction system icing can lead to engine roughness
Engine Roughness Checklist
Without a direct indication of icing, engine roughness is likely the first sign of the problem
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Directs you to open the alternate air intake
Door or Window Opening in Flight
Open Door Checklist
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
General Information (POH takes precedence)
Concentrate on flying the plane, an open door seldom compromises the ability of the plane to fly
Do not rush to land the plane if the door opens during lift off
Climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it
The Piper Archer does have a checklist to close the door in flight. Do not lose control of the aircraft trying to close the door. Fly the plane first.
Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then settle partially closed
A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim
Electric Pitch Trim Failure
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Electric Pitch Trim Runaway
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Basically, maintain control, disengage the autopilot/trim system and turn it off (pull CB)
Fly first!
Autopilot Out-Of-Trim
Reference checklist in Section 3 of the POH Flight Operations
Do not attempt to overpower the autopilot – the servos will oppose and trim opposite your input
Flap Malfunction
General (no specific procedures in the Archer POH)
Total Flap Failure
This will necessitate a no flap approach and landing
Requires substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
Flown in a relatively nose-high attitude as compared to flaps extended
Can make the runway difficult to see
Wider, longer pattern may be necessary to avoid diving to lose altitude & building up speed
Tendency to float considerably during roundout
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys/retracts while the other remains in position
The problem is indicated by a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countering
Countered with opposite aileron
Yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side will require opposite rudder
Aileron and opposite rudder results in a crossed control situation
Close to full aileron may be necessary at the reduced airspeed to maintain wings level
Do not attempt to land with a crosswind from the side of the deployed flap
Additional roll control to counteract the crosswind may not be available
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
Wing with the retracted flap will stall earlier - possible crossed control stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher-than-normal airspeed
Use POH published flaps speeds and adjust for the higher landing distance
Pressurization Malfunction
Not applicable for the Piper Archer, but in general, descend and/or use supplemental oxygen
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
Understanding different emergencies and how to deal with them is obviously important as you will always be prepared and be able to react quickly in the event one of these emergencies occurs.
XII.C. Piper Arrow (PA-28R-201)
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story

Wouldn’t it be fun to be flying one day and experience a problem that you have no idea how to deal with? Of course not, that’s why it’s important to understand your equipment and the proper procedures associated.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Systems and equipment malfunctions involve knowing how to handle problems that may occur in the airplane to provide as safe a flight as possible.
Why

The key to successful management of an emergency situation, and/or preventing a non-normal situation from progressing into a true emergency, is a thorough knowledge of, and adherence to, the necessary procedures.
How:
Smoke, Fire, or Both, During Ground or Flight Operations
Ground Operations
Engine Fire During Start - Usually the result of overpriming
Procedures
The first attempt to extinguish the fire is to try to start the engine and draw the excess fuel back into the induction system
Fire Prior to Engine Start – Move the mixture to idle cut-off, open the throttle and crank the engine
This is an attempt to draw the fire back into the engine
If the Engine has Started – Continue operating to try to pull the fire into the engine
In either case (above), if the fire continues more than a few seconds, the fire should be extinguished by the best available external means
The fuel selector valves should be off and the mixture at idle cut-off if an external fire extinguishing method is to be used
Checklist
Flight Operations
General
Presence of fire is noted through smoke, smell, and/or heat in the cabin
The source of the fire must be promptly identified. Check for the source of the fire first
Identifiers like instrument readings, characters of the smoke (smell, color, location), etc.
Electrical Fire in Flight
Engine Fire in Flight
Rough Running Engine or Partial Power Loss
General
Engine roughness may be caused by dirt in the injector nozzles, induction system icing, or ignition problems
Procedure
Loss of Engine Oil Pressure
General
Can be a partial or total loss of oil pressure
Partial Loss
Usually indicates a malfunction in the oil pressure regulating system, and a landing should be made as soon as possible to investigate the cause and prevent engine damage
Complete Loss
May signify oil exhaustion or may be the result of a faulty gauge
In either case, proceed toward the nearest airport and be prepared for a forced landing. If the problem is not a pressure gauge malfunction, the engine may stop suddenly
Maintain altitude until such time as a dead stick landing can be accomplished
Don’t change power settings unnecessarily, this may hasten complete power loss

Depending on the circumstances, it may be advisable to make an off airport landing while power is still available, particularly if other indication of actual oil pressure loss, such as sudden increases in temperatures, or oil smoke, are apparent, and an airport is not close
Procedures
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine, and can be caused by blocked fuel lines or empty tanks
The most probable cause of loss of fuel flow/pressure is either fuel depletion or failure of the engine driven fuel pump
If loss of fuel flow/pressure occurs, check that the fuel selector is on a tank containing fuel and turn on the electric fuel pump
Unless recognized immediately, the most likely course of action is to run the Engine Roughness checklist, or Engine Power Loss in Flight checklist
If the engine roughness/failure was caused by fuel exhaustion, it may take up to 10 seconds for the empty fuel lines to fill with fuel and power to be restored
In the case of fuel starvation, a power off landing will be necessary using the Power Off Landing checklist
Plan ahead while on the ground, and monitor fuel while in flight to prevent fuel starvation
If at any point during flight the fuel required is not in line with the fuel available create a new plan. Divert immediately if necessary, don’t rely on hope!
Engine Overheat
General
The oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Watch the oil pressure gauge for an accompanying loss of pressure
A steady rise in oil temperature is a sign of trouble. Land at the nearest airport and let a mechanic investigate the problem
Rising oil temperature may be the result of a low oil level, and obstruction in the oil cooler, damaged or improper baffle seals, a defective gauge, or other causes
High Oil Temperature Procedures
Land at the nearest airport and investigate the problem
Prepare for power off landing
Causes and Corrective Action
Hydraulic Malfunction
General Brake Failure Procedures – Not in the POH
Symptoms of impending brake failure:
Gradual decrease in braking action after brake application
Noisy or dragging brakes
Soft or spongy pedals
Excessive brake travel
Weak braking action
If during taxi or landing roll, braking action decreases let up on the pedals and the reapply the brakes with heavy pressure
If the brakes become spongy or pedal travel increases, pumping the pedals should build brake pressure
If one brake becomes weak or fails, use the other brake sparingly while using opposite rudder, as required, to offset the good brake
If both brakes have failed, select the longest landing surface available. Make a controlled landing without excessive float and slow the aircraft straight ahead with aerodynamic braking
Electrical Malfunction
Alternator Failure
Electrical Overload

If abnormally high alternator output is observed (more than 20 amps above known electrical load for the operating conditions) it may be caused by a low battery, a battery fault, or other abnormal electrical load
Electrical Overload Checklist
Induction Icing
General
As air is ingested through the engine intakes, the moisture can freeze inside the induction system, reducing or stopping the flow of combustible air to the engine
Ice can also form on the exterior of the airplane, and clog the air intake openings
The Engine Roughness checklist is likely the most applicable checklist, especially if the onset of icing has not been noticed by the pilot
This checklist will direct the pilot to open the alternate air source
Exit the icing – Run the checklist and attempt to exit the icing (climb/descent to better conditions, turn around, ATC vectors, etc.)
Door or Window Opening in Flight
POH Amplified Emergency Procedures
The cabin door is double latched so the changes of it opening during flight are remote
However, a partially open door will not affect the normal flight characteristics of the aircraft and a normal landing can be made with the door open
If both latches are open, the door will trail slightly open, and airspeed will be reduced slightly
Open Door Checklist
In the event of an inadvertent door opening in flight or on takeoff, adhere to the following general information:
Concentrate on flying the plane, an open door seldom compromises the ability of the plane to fly
Do not rush to land the plane if the door opens during lift off
Climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it
The Piper Archer does have a checklist to close the door in flight. Do not lose control of the aircraft trying to close the door. Fly the plane first.
Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then settle partially closed
A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim
In case of Electric Trim Malfunction (if installed, and depending on the system installed)
Flap Malfunction
General (no specific procedures in the Archer POH)
Total Flap Failure
This will necessitate a no flap approach and landing
This will require substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
The airplane must be flown in a relatively nose-high attitude as compared to flaps extended
This can make the runway difficult to see
A wider, longer pattern may be necessary to avoid diving to lose altitude and building up airspeed
The airplane will tend to float considerably during roundout
If only flaps are unavailable, raise the approach airspeed 10 knots and maintain a flat approach angle
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys/retracts while the other remains in position
The problem is indicated by a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countering
Countered with opposite aileron
The yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side will require opposite rudder
Aileron and opposite rudder results in a crossed control situation
Almost full aileron may be necessary at the reduced airspeed to maintain wings level
Therefore, do not attempt to land with a crosswind from the side of the deployed flap
The additional roll control to counteract the crosswind may not be available
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
The wing with the retracted flap will stall much earlier - possible crossed control stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher-than-normal airspeed
Pressurization Malfunction
Not applicable for the Piper Arrow, but in general descend or use supplemental oxygen
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
Understanding different emergencies and how to deal with them is obviously important as you will always be prepared and be able to react quickly in the event one of these emergencies occurs.

The first attempt to extinguish the fire is to try to start the engine and draw the excess fuel back into the induction system
Fire Prior to Engine Start – Move the mixture to idle cut-off, open the throttle and crank the engine 
This is an attempt to draw the fire back into the engine
If the Engine has Started – Continue operating to try to pull the fire into the engine
In either case (above), if the fire continues more than a few seconds, the fire should be extinguished by the best available external means
The fuel selector valves should be off and the mixture at idle cut-off if an external fire extinguishing method is to be used

Ammeter: Check to verify inoperative alternator
Loss of alternator output is detected through zero reading on the ammeter. Before executing the following procedure, ensure that the reading is zero and not merely low by actuating an electrically powered device (like the landing light). If no increase in the ammeter reading is noted, alternator failure can be assumed
If ammeter shows zero:

Reduce electrical loads to minimum:
ALT circuit breaker: Check and reset as required
ALT switch: On
Switching the alternator off and then on attempts to reset the overvoltage relay. If the problem was caused by a momentary overvoltage condition (16.5 volts or more), this procedure should return the ammeter to normal operation.
If power not restored (ammeter still indicates zero), or the alternator will not remain reset:
ALT switch: Off
If alternator output cannot be restored, reduce electrical loads and land as soon as practical. The battery is the only remaining source of electrical power

Electrical load: Reduce
If alternator loads are reduced:
ALT switch: Off
Land as soon as practical. The battery is the only remaining source of power. Anticipate complete electrical failure

If ammeter shows zero:
ALTR switch: Off
Reduce electrical loads to minimum:
ALTR FIELD circuit breaker: Check and reset as required
ALTR switch: On
Switching the alternator off and then on attempts to reset the overvoltage relay. If the problem was caused by a momentary overvoltage condition (16.5 volts or more), this procedure should return the ammeter to normal operation.
If power not restored (ammeter still indicates zero), or the alternator will not remain reset:
ALTR switch: Off
If alternator output cannot be restored, reduce electrical loads and land as soon as practical. The battery is the only remaining source of electrical power

BATT MASTR: Switch: Off
If ammeter reading does NOT decrease:
ALTR Switch: Off
Land as soon as possible. Use Emergency Landing Gear Extension to lower the gear
If ammeter reading DOES decrease:
BATT MASTR Switch: On
Ammeter: Monitor
If ammeter reading does NOT begin to decrease within five minutes:
BATT MASTR Switch: Off
Land as soon as possible
If the battery is depleted, the landing gear must be lowered using the emergency extension procedure. The gear position lights will be inoperative
If ammeter reading DOES begin to decrease within five minutes:
Proceed with flight
Ammeter: Monitor

To close the door in flight:
Slow the aircraft to 87 KIAS
Cabin Vents: Close
Storm Window: Open
If upper latch is open: Latch
If side latch is open: Pull on armrest while moving latch handle to latched position
If both latches are open: Latch side latch then top latch

Trim Interrupt/AP Disconnect switch: Depress and hold throughout recovery
Trim Master switch: Off
Circuit Breaker: Pull
Trim Interrupt/AP Disconnect switch: Release
Aircraft: Retrim manually
Leave system off until corrected
extra_detail_lessons.full_text:
XII.C. Systems and Equipment Malfunctions
Select the aircraft Systems and Equipment Malfunctions lesson from the Navigation Pane, or use the links below:
GENERIC
Generic Aircraft Malfunctions
CESSNA
Cessna 152
Cessna 172S G1000
CIRRUS
Cirrus SR20
DIAMOND
Diamond DA20
Diamond DA40
PIPER
Piper Archer II (PA-28-181)
Piper Archer III (PA-28-181)
Piper Arrow (PA-28R-201)
XII.C. Generic
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Wouldn’t it be fun to be flying one day and experience a problem that you have no idea how to deal with? Of course not, that’s why it’s important to understand your equipment and the proper procedures associated.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Systems and equipment malfunctions involve the knowledge and procedures to handle problems that may occur in the airplane.
Why
The key to successful management of an emergency, and/or preventing a non-normal situation from progressing into a true emergency, is a thorough knowledge of, and adherence to, the necessary procedures.
How:
Note: This lesson provides generic procedures & malfunction discussions. Always follow the POH procedures.
Malfunction Procedures (MATL)
Maintain Aircraft Control
Fly the airplane
Get to a safe flight state (straight-and-level, etc.)
Trim the aircraft and turn on the autopilot, if possible
Maintaining control continues throughout the malfunction
Do not let the issue, checklists, etc. distract from flying the airplane
Divide attention between flying and checklists/procedures
RM: Distractions can lead to an undesired aircraft state (UAS) 				AI.XII.C.R4
Can quickly amplify the malfunction already being dealt with
The malfunction could also be the reason for the UAS
Maintaining control is the top priority – in the case of an UAS:
Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize as required
Understand the specific malfunction may limit or prevent recovery
Further emphasizes the need to maintain control
Analyze the Situation
Indications, lights, sounds, visual (i.e., smoke, leaks, fire, etc.), smells, etc.
Use all available information to determine the issue
Take the Proper Action
Apply any memory items
RM: Checklist usage – Use the appropriate checklist from the POH 				AI.XII.C.R2
Checklist is the safest, most effective way to handle the problem
Don’t go rogue and make up your own procedure/guess
Potential to not fix the problem and/or cause other problems
Land, as conditions require/permit
Based on the emergency, decide on a landing area (divert, field, ditching, etc.)
This may have to occur in conjunction with the checklist(s)
Power Loss 												AI.XII.C.K1
Rough running engine:
Oil Pressure Malfunctions
High Oil Pressure
Possible Cause - Cold oil or possible internal plugging
Corrective Action - If cold, allow the engine to warm, if not, reduce power and land ASAP
Low Oil Pressure
Possible Cause – Broken pressure relief valve, insufficient oil, burned out bearings
Corrective Action – Land as soon as possible or feather the propeller and stop the engine (multi-engine)
Fluctuating Oil Pressure
Possible Cause – Low oil supply, loose oil lines, defective pressure relief valve
Corrective Action – Land as soon as possible or feather propeller and stop engine (multi-engine)
Engine Overheat
The oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine, and can be caused by blocked lines or empty tanks
In general, turn on boost pumps, switch tanks, verify fuel is on, adjust mixture
Electrical Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2a
Electrical Power
Generally, power comes from a generator or alternator
If the generator/alternator fails, typically a battery provides power for a limited amount of time
Battery Time
The higher the amperage load (electrical draw) on the battery, the faster the energy gets consumed
Ex: 25-amp hour battery can produce 5 amps per hour for 5 hours
Increasing to 10 amps, it may only last 2 hours
40 amps may discharge the battery in 10-15 mins
Battery condition matters
Over time, power is reduced due to internal resistance
Very important to shed non-essential loads to provide maximum time
Consumers
See picture to right for average amperage
Gear and flaps use significant amounts of power
Using them may result in a total loss of power
Procedures
Follow the applicable checklist(s) in the POH
Reduce electrical load
Fly on the backup instruments
Generic Steps
Shed all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Can vary based on the situation (day/night, VMC/IMC)
Notify ATC immediately – Request vectors for landing at the nearest suitable airport
Expect a no-flap landing and manual gear extension
Vacuum/Pressure Malfunctions 									AI.XII.C.K2b
What’s Lost?
Heading Indicator, Attitude Indicator, and/or Turn Coordinator
Traditionally, turn coordinators use a different power source than the heading / attitude indicators
Ex. Vacuum for the attitude and heading gyros, and electric for the turn coordinator
If the heading & attitude indicators fail, the turn coordinator is still usable, and vice versa
Failure results from a loss of the suction or pressure source (vacuum failure)
As the gyroscopes slow down, they will begin to wander, displaying incorrect information
Can be slow and insidious
Many small aircraft do not have a warning system for vacuum failure
Look for vacuum failure indications – monitor the vacuum pressure gauge
Compare the Attitude Indicator with the Turn Coordinator and VSI
Along with providing pitch / bank information, this compares the static, suction, and electric systems
Identify the failed component(s) and use the remaining functional instruments to maintain control
Assess the situation - when and where to land may vary based on the conditions and failure(s)
Day VMC with backup instruments may allow the pilot to return to their home field
Night, reduced visibility, or minimal horizon may require an emergency and landing at the closest field
Pitot Static Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2c
General
Errors in the ASI and VSI almost always indicate a pitot blockage, static blockage, or both
Moisture, ice, dirt, insects, etc. can cause a blockages
Always preflight the pitot tube and static ports
Blocked Pitot System
Pitot system measures the difference between ram air pressure in the pitot tube and static air pressure from the static port
Static pressure is vented to instrument casing
Ram air is connected to a diaphragm in the case
Ram air blocked, with drain hole open
Air already in the system vents through the drain hole and remaining pressure in the pitot tube drops to match the outside (static) air pressure
Airspeed decreases to zero as ram air pressure and static pressure become equal
Not an instantaneous drop, but happens quickly
Ram air blocked, and drain hole blocked
Big Picture
Airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter
Ram air pressure in the pitot tube is trapped
Accelerating/decelerating does not affect indications
Static pressure changes with altitude
In a climb
Ram air pressure remains constant
Static pressure decreases
Diaphragm expands, just like would happen with an increase in ram air pressure/acceleration
Airspeed increases as altitude increases
In a descent
Ram air pressure remains constant
Static pressure increases
Diaphragm contracts, just like would happen with a decrease in ram air pressure/deceleration
Airspeed decreases as altitude decreases
Airspeed acts like an altimeter, increasing in a climb and decreasing in a descent
Blocked Static System
Static system blocked, with pitot tube open
Airspeed operates but is inaccurate
When above the altitude where the static port(s) were blocked, airspeed indicates lower than actual
Trapped pressure is higher than normal for the altitude
When at a lower altitude, airspeed indicates higher than actual
Trapped pressure is lower than normal for that altitude
Altimeter freezes at the altitude where the block occurred
Vertical Speed shows a continuous zero indication
Alternate Static Source
Provides alternate source of static pressure in the case the primary becomes blocked
Normally inside the flight deck
Cabin pressure is lower than exterior pressure due to venturi effect of air flowing around the fuselage
Instrument indications when the alternate static source is used:
Altimeter indicates slightly higher than actual
Airspeed indicates greater than actual
Vertical speed shows a momentary climb and then stabilizes if altitude is constant
Electronic Flight Display (EFD) Malfunction 								AI.XII.C.K2d
In the case of an EFD failure, the system reverts to a composite, reversionary mode
Moving map is eliminated
PFD and engine instruments are combined on the remaining screen
Pilots often become overly reliant on the moving map
What should be a supplementary source of data becomes a primary navigation tool
Significant loss of situational awareness if the pilot is not prepared for this failure
Stay Prepared
Follow the flight on an enroute chart while monitoring the moving map
Have a Chart Supplement to prevent losing access to airport information
Flap Malfunction 											AI.XII.C.K2e
Total Flap Failure (no flap approach and landing)
Requires substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
Losing altitude is more difficult so a wider, longer pattern may be necessary
Flown in a relatively nose-high attitude compared to flaps extended
On final, this can make it difficult to see the runway
Can lead to errors in judgement of height/distance and cause the perception the plane is close to a stall
Landing
Airplane is slightly less stable in pitch and roll axes with power reduced and flaps retracted
Tend to float during roundout
Don’t force the plane onto the ground
Don’t flare excessively as it risks a tail strike
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys or retracts while the other remains in position
Indicated by a roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countered with opposite aileron
Yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side requires opposite rudder
Almost full aileron may be necessary at reduced airspeeds to maintain wings level
Do not attempt to land with a cross-wind from the side of the deployed flap
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
The wing with the retracted flap will stall earlier - possible cross-controlled stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher-than-normal airspeed
Hydraulic Malfunction  										AI.XII.C.K2e
If the hydraulic pump were to fail, there are alternate means to raise/lower the gear
Some airplanes will automatically lower the gear
Landing Gear Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2e
Alternate gear extension procedure
If this does not solve the problem, a gear up landing is required
Considerations
Airport with crash and rescue facilities
A smooth, hard runway surface tends to cause less damage than a rough, unimproved grass strip
The hard surface does create sparks that could ignite fuel
Can request for the runway to be foamed, if available
Burn off excess fuel
Reduced landing speed and chance of fire
If the malfunction is limited to one leg, consume as much fuel from that side as practicable
Reduced weight on that side allows you to delay contact with the surface until the last moment
Reduced impact speed = reduced damage
Landing the Airplane
One Leg Retracted
Land in a nose-high attitude with wings level
As airspeed slows, apply aileron to keep the unsupported wing airborne as long as possible
After touchdown, the airplane will veer strongly in the direction of the faulty gear leg/dragging wing
Use full opposite rudder and aggressive braking to maintain some degree of directional control
On a narrow runway, or one with ditches/obstacles on the edges, landing with all gear up may be safer
Nose Wheel Retracted
Hold the nose off the ground until almost full-up elevator is applied
Release back pressure to allow the nose to slowly settle to the surface
Applying full back pressure results in the nose abruptly dropping to the surface
Can result in burrowing and/or additional damage
Try to gently set the nose on the ground
Do not apply brakes unless necessary to avoid a collision with obstacles
Main Gear Retracted (Nose extended)
Initial contact should be made on the aft fuselage with a nose high attitude
Helps to prevent porpoising and/or wheelbarrowing
Allow the nose-wheel to gradually touchdown
Use nose-wheel steering as necessary
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim 									AI.XII.C.K2f
Grip the controls and maintain control of the plane while disengaging the electric trim system
Disengage button, circuit breaker, etc.
If the reason for the runaway trim is obvious and has been resolved, engage the breaker
Smoke & Fire  											AI.XII.C.K3
In any fire, it is essential the source is discovered first
Identifying the source allows the pilot to fight the fire most effectively
Identify/shutdown the faulty component, use the extinguisher effectively, run the proper checklist, etc.
In-Flight Smoke/Fire
Engine Fire
Usually caused by a failure allowing a combustible substance to contact a hot surface
Indicated by smoke / flames from cowling; and / or discoloration, bubbling, melting of cowling
Unless the POH says otherwise, 1st step should be to shut off fuel
If the flames are put out, do not attempt to restart the engine
Perform an emergency landing
Keep in mind:
There may be severe structural damage and control could be lost at any time
Airplane may still be on fire and susceptible to explosion
Airplane is expendable and the only thing that matters is the safety of those onboard
Electrical Fires
First indication is usually the distinct odor of burning insulation
Try to identify the problem by checking circuit breakers, lights, instruments, avionics
If it cannot be detected, the battery master and generator should be turned off
Any materials which have been ignited may continue to burn
If power is essential for the flight, attempt to identify / isolate the faulty circuit:
Electrical master off, then all individual electrical switches off
Electrical master on
Turn on electrical switches one at a time, waiting after each switch to check for signs of fire
Turn off / do not use any equipment that restarts the fire. Other equipment can be used
Cabin Fires
Usually result from smoking, electrical system malfunctions, and heating system malfunctions
Two immediate demands:
Attacking the fire, and getting the airplane safely on the ground as quickly as possible
In general, identify and shutdown the cause of the fire
Smoke can often be cleared by opening air vents – only after using the fire extinguisher
If smoke increases, immediately close them
Windows can also be used to help clear smoke
Use oxygen if the smoke is severe; initiate an immediate descent
Ground Smoke / Fire
Engine Fire / Smoke - Shut down the engine, turn off the electrics and evacuate the airplane
Electrical Fire / Smoke - Immediately turn off the master switch, and shutdown the engine
Use the fire extinguisher and evacuate as necessary
Door or Window Opening in Flight									AI.XII.C.K5
Follow the POH procedures. In general, adhere to the following:
Concentrate on flying the plane, an open door seldom compromises the ability of the plane to fly
Do not rush to land (climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing)
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it
Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then settle partially closed
A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed
Pressurization Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K4
Descend or use supplemental oxygen (emergency descent)
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression
Other Malfunctions (supplemental oxygen, deicing, etc.) 						AI.XII.C.K4
Reference the POH and/or user’s manual for specific procedures
Common Errors 											AI.XII.C.K6
Inaccurate diagnoses of the malfunction
Use of an improper checklist/procedure
Lack of control throughout the malfunction
Fixation on the malfunction at the expense of the aircraft & safe flight
RM: Hazards
Startle Response										AI.XII.C.R1
Uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflex, raised heart rate, blood pressure, etc. elicited by exposure to a sudden intense event that violates a pilot’s expectations
Protect against startle response through scenario-based training incorporating realistic distractions
The pilot should react in a calm, controlled manner and:
Maintain aircraft control
Analyze the situation
Take the proper action
Land, as conditions require/permit
Reactions or inputs outside of checklists may likely aggravate the situation
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization		 				AI.XII.C.R3
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem and fix it
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Especially important to avoid distractions in an emergency with numerous tasks to manage
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
High task load during an emergency can lead to a loss of SA
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft & malfunction, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention for more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Organization is especially important in situations like this – many tasks, little time
“Attack the closest alligator”
When tasks are piling up, handle the most threatening problem
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
Understanding different emergencies and how to deal with them is obviously important as you will always be prepared and be able to react quickly in the event one of these emergencies occurs.
XII.C. DA20
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Wouldn’t it be fun to be flying one day and experience a problem that you have no idea how to deal with? Of course not, that’s why it’s important to understand your equipment and the proper procedures associated.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Systems and equipment malfunctions involve knowing how to handle problems that may occur in the airplane to provide as safe a flight as possible.
Why
The key to successful management of an emergency situation, and/or preventing a non-normal situation from progressing into a true emergency, is a thorough knowledge of, and adherence to, the necessary procedures.
How:
*The following procedures are from the DA20 POH, changes will have to be made for your aircraft
Smoke, Fire, or Both, During Ground or Flight Operations
In-Flight Smoke/Fire - In any fire, it is essential the source is discovered first
Engine Fire
Usually caused by a failure allowing a combustible substance to contact a hot surface
Checklist
If the flames are put out, do not attempt to restart the engine
Perform an emergency landing
Keep in mind that
There may be severe structural damage and control could be lost at any time
The airplane may still be on fire and susceptible to explosion
The airplane is expendable and the only thing that matters is the safety of those onboard
Electrical Fires
Indication is usually the distinct odor of burning insulation
Checklist
GEN/BAT Master: OFF
Cabin Air:  OPEN
Fire Extinguisher: Use only if smoke development continues
If the fire is extinguished and electric power is required to continue the flight:
Avionics Master: OFF
Electrically Powered Equipment: OFF
Restore electrical power systematically allowing time to monitor the
system voltmeter and amp meter-Watch carefully for smoke
Try to identify the faulty circuit by checking circuit breakers, lights, instruments, and avionics
If it cannot be detected, the battery master switch and generator should be turned off
However, any materials which have been ignited may continue to burn
If there is smoke in the flight deck, open the windows
Cabin Fires
Usually result from:
Careless smoking on the part of the pilot and/or passengers
Electrical system malfunctions
Heating system malfunctions
Two immediate demands:
Attacking the fire
Getting the airplane safely on the ground as quickly as possible
Checklist
Ground Smoke/Fire
Engine Fire/Smoke
Checklist
Electrical Fire/Smoke
If smoke in the cabin indicates an electrical fire, immediately turn off the master switch
Checklist
GEN/BAT Master: OFF
In Engine is running
Rough Running Engine or Partial Power Loss
Checklist
Loss of Engine Oil Pressure
High Oil Pressure
Possible Cause - Cold oil or possible internal plugging
Corrective Action - If cold, allow the engine to warm, if not, reduce power and land ASAP
Low Oil Pressure
Possible Cause - Broken Pressure Relief Valve, Insufficient Oil, Burned Out Bearings
Corrective Action - Land ASAP or feather the prop and stop engine
Checklist
Oil Temp: CHECK
If Pressure drops below Green Arc but Temp is normal: LAND AT NEAREST FIELD
If Pressure drops below Green Arc and Temp is rising: REDUCE THROTTLE TO MIN REQ POWER
Be prepared for engine failure and emergency landing
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine, and can be caused by blocked lines or empty tanks
Check the fuel flow gauge
Fuel Shutoff: OPEN
Mixture: FULL RICH
Electric Fuel Pump: ON
Check the fuel flow gauge again
Engine Overheat
The oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Causes and Corrective Action
Hydraulic Malfunction (not applicable to DA20)
If the hydraulic pump were to fail, there are manual means to raise/lower the gear
Some airplanes will automatically lower the gear (DA42)
Electrical Malfunction
The generator/alternator is the cause of most electrical system failures (indicated on the ammeter)
Once the generator goes offline, the only electrical source remaining is the battery
The battery although may have very little time available
Electrically powered gear and flaps use up power at rates much greater than most other equipment
Selecting these motors on a partially depleted battery could result in immediate loss of power
Steps
Turn off all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Save as much power as possible
Notify ATC immediately and request vectors for a landing at the nearest airport
Expect to make a no flap landing, and anticipate a manual gear extension
Checklist
Total Electrical Failure
Generator Failure (GEN. Annunciator Light Illuminated)
GEN/BAT Master: Cycle Generator Master Switch OFF - ON
Generator Circuit Breaker: RESET, if tripped
Generator Control Breaker: RESET, if tripped
If GEN cannot be brought online: Switch off all non-flight essential electrical consumers
Monitor the Ammeter and Voltmeter
Land at the nearest airport
Low Voltage Indication (Needle in yellow arc) While on the Ground
Engine RPM: Increase RPM until needle is in the Green Arc (Should occur before 1100 RPM)
Non-Flight Essential Electrical Consumers: Switch OFF consumers until in the Green Arc
If needle remains in the yellow arc, and the ammeter is indicating left of center (discharge), discontinue any flight activity
Low Voltage Indication (needle in yellow arc) While in the Air
Non-Flight Essential Electrical Consumers: OFF
If needle stays in the yellow arc, and the ammeter indicates a discharge, use GEN FAILURE
Induction Icing
As air is ingested through the engine intakes, the moisture can freeze inside the induction system, reducing or stopping the flow of combustible air to the engine
Ice can also form on the exterior of the airplane, and clog the air intake openings
Corrective Action
Use the Alternate Air source
Icing Checklist
Leave icing area (change altitude or flight direction to reach a higher temp)
Continue to move the control surfaces to maintain mobility
Alternate Air: ON
Increase RPM to avoid icing of prop blades
Cabin Heat: ON DEFROST
Door or Window Opening in Flight
In the event of an inadvertent door opening in flight or on takeoff, adhere to the following:
Concentrate on flying the plane, an open door seldom compromises the ability of the plane to fly
Do not rush to land the plane if the door opens during lift off
Climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it
Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then settle partially closed
A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim
Checklist
Control Stick: Grip stick and maintain control of the airplane
Trim Motor Circuit Breaker: PULL the breaker
Rocker Switch: Check if depressed
If the reason for the runaway trim is obvious and has been resolved, engage the breaker
Flap Malfunction
Total Flap Failure
This will necessitate a no flap approach and landing
This will require substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
The airplane must be flown in a relatively nose-high attitude as compared to flaps extended
This can make the runway difficult to see
A wider, longer pattern may be necessary to avoid diving to lose altitude and building up airspeed
The airplane will tend to float considerably during roundout
If only flaps are unavailable, raise the approach airspeed 10 knots and maintain a flat approach angle
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys/retracts while the other remains in position
The problem is indicated by a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countering
Countered with opposite aileron
The yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side will require opposite rudder
Aileron and opposite rudder results in a cross controlled situation
Almost full aileron may be necessary at the reduced airspeed to maintain wings level
Therefore, do not attempt to land with a cross-wind from the side of the deployed flap
The additional roll control to counteract the cross-wind may not be available
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
The wing with the retracted flap will stall much earlier - possible cross-controlled stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher than normal airspeed
Pressurization Malfunction
Descend or use supplemental oxygen
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
Understanding different emergencies and how to deal with them is obviously important as you will always be prepared and be able to react quickly in the event one of these emergencies occurs.
XII.C. Cessna 152
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Wouldn’t it be fun to be flying one day and experience a problem that you have no idea how to deal with? Of course not, that’s why it’s important to understand your equipment and the proper procedures associated.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Systems and equipment malfunctions involve knowing how to handle problems that may occur in the aircraft to provide as safe a flight as possible.
Why
The key to successful management of an emergency situation, and/or preventing a non-normal situation from progressing into a true emergency, is a thorough knowledge of, and adherence to, the necessary procedures.
How:
Smoke, Fire, or Both, During Ground or Flight Operations
In-Flight Smoke/Fire - In any fire, it is essential the source is discovered first
Engine Fire in Flight
Usually caused by a failure allowing a combustible substance to contact a hot surface
Checklist
If fire is not extinguished at 85 KIAS, increase glide speed to find an airspeed which will provide an incombustible mixture
Perform an emergency landing
Keep in mind that
There may be severe structural damage and control could be lost at any time
The airplane may still be on fire and susceptible to explosion
The airplane is expendable and the only thing that matters is the safety of those onboard
Electrical Fire in Flight
Indication is usually the distinct odor of burning insulation (acrid)
Checklist
After discharging an extinguished in a closed cabin, ventilate the cabin
If the fire returns when restoring power (i.e. the system that received power is a cause of the fire), immediately turn off the switch/system and fight the fire
Wing Fire
The POH does not specify whether this checklist applies inflight or on the ground
Basically, remove all power sources from the wing
Checklist
Perform a sideslip to keep the flames away from the fuel tank and cabin, and land as soon as possible, with flaps retracted
Cabin Fire
POH does not specify whether this checklist applies inflight or on the ground
Usually result from:
Careless smoking on the part of the pilot and/or passengers
Electrical system malfunctions
Heating system malfunctions
Two immediate demands:
Attacking the fire
Getting the airplane safely on the ground as quickly as possible
Checklist
Ground Smoke/Fire
During Start on Ground
Checklist
Rough Running Engine or Partial Power Loss
No specific rough running engine checklist, but in the Amplified Emergency Procedures section the POH references Rough Engine Operation or Loss of Power
Carburetor Icing
A gradual loss of RPM and eventual engine roughness may result from the formation of carburetor ice
To clear the ice:
Apply full throttle
Pull the carb heat knob full out until the engine runs smoothly
Remove the carb heat and readjust the throttle
If conditions require continued use of carb heat in flight, use the minimum amount of heat necessary to prevent ice from forming and lean the mixture slightly for smoothest engine operation
Spark Plug Fouling
Slight engine roughness can be caused by spark plug fouling (carbon or lead deposit on the spark plug)
Verify by turning the mags switch momentarily from Both to either L or R. An obvious power loss in single mag operation is evidence of spark plug or magneto trouble
Procedure (assuming spark plugs are the issue. Magento malfunction is described below)
Lean the mixture to the recommended lean setting for cruise flight

Electrical Malfunction
General
The generator/alternator is the cause of most electrical system failures
Once the generator goes offline, the only electrical source remaining is the battery
The battery although may have very little time available
Electrically powered gear and flaps use up power at rates much greater than most other equipment
Selecting these motors on a partially depleted battery could result in immediate loss of power
Malfunctions in the electrical system can be detected through regular monitoring of the ammeter and low-voltage warning light
The cause of these malfunctions is usually difficult to determine
A broken alternator drive belt or wiring is the most likely cause of alternator failures
A damaged or improperly adjusted alternator control unit can also cause malfunctions
Electrical power malfunctions generally fall into two categories:
Excessive Rate of Charge
After 30 minutes of cruise flight, the main battery ammeter should be indicating less than 2 needle widths of charging current. If the charging current remains above this value on a long flight, the battery electrolyte could overheat and evaporate
Electronic components can be adversely affected by higher than normal voltage
The Alternator Control Unit should disconnect the alternator if the charge increases to more than 31.5 volts
If the ACU does not operate correctly, the alternator should be turned off, alternator circuit breaker pulled, nonessential electrical equipment turned off, and the flight terminated as soon as practical
Insufficient Rate of Charge
i.e. the alternator is not providing the necessary charge
If the over-voltage sensor shuts down the alternator, or the alternator circuit breaker trips a discharge will be show on the ammeter followed by the low-voltage warning light
This may be a nuisance trip, attempt to energize the alternator system by:
Turning off the radios
Checking the alternator circuit breaker is in
Turning the master switch off and back on
If this doesn’t reset the system, there is an alternator system problem
The flight should be terminated and the current drain on the battery minimized to extend the amount of time on battery power
If the emergency occurs at night, power must be conserved for later use of the landing light and flaps
General Steps to any electrical malfunction
Turn off all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Save as much power as possible
Notify ATC immediately and request vectors for a landing at the nearest airport
Expect to make a no flap landing, and anticipate a manual gear extension

Idle Power Engine Roughness
An excessively rich idle fuel flow may cause low speed engine roughness during flight
During most in-flight low engine speeds (power off stalls, approach to landing, etc.), the mixture control is normally in the full-rich position. However, to improve engine roughness (caused by an improperly adjusted fuel servo) during low engine speeds while in flight, you should lean the mixture.
You may also have to lean the fuel mixture if this low engine speed results in power loss and you need to restart the engine during flight.
In all cases, you should land the airplane at the nearest airport for repairs if low speed engine roughness requires you to adjust the fuel mixture control to improve engine operation.
Engine Driven Fuel Pump Failure
Failure of the engine driven fuel pump will be shown by a sudden reduction in the fuel flow indication immediately before a loss of power while operating from a fuel tank containing adequate fuel
Procedure
Immediately set the Fuel Pump switch to On to restore engine power
The flight should be terminated as soon as practical
Excessive Fuel Vapor
Fuel vapor in the fuel injection system is most likely to occur on the ground, typically during prolonged taxi operations when operating at higher altitudes and/or in unusually warm temperatures
Excessive fuel vapor accumulation is shown by fuel flow indicator fluctuations greater than 1 gal per hour
This condition, with leaner mixtures or with larger fluctuations, can result in power surges, and if not corrected, may cause power loss
Procedure
To slow vapor formation and stabilize fuel flow on the ground or in the air, set the Fuel Pump switch to On and adjust the mixture for smooth engine operation
If vapor symptoms continue, select the opposite fuel tank
When fuel flow stabilizes, set the Fuel Pump to Off and adjust the mixture as desired

Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it
The Piper Archer does have a checklist to close the door in flight. Do not lose control of the aircraft trying to close the door. Fly the plane first.
Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then settle partially closed
A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim
In case of Electric Trim Malfunction (if installed, and depending on the system installed)
Flap Malfunction
General (no specific procedures in the Archer POH)
Total Flap Failure
This will necessitate a no flap approach and landing
This will require substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
The airplane must be flown in a relatively nose-high attitude as compared to flaps extended
This can make the runway difficult to see
A wider, longer pattern may be necessary to avoid diving to lose altitude and building up airspeed
The airplane will tend to float considerably during roundout
If only flaps are unavailable, raise the approach airspeed 10 knots and maintain a flat approach angle
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys/retracts while the other remains in position
The problem is indicated by a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countering
Countered with opposite aileron
The yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side will require opposite rudder
Aileron and opposite rudder results in a crossed control situation
Almost full aileron may be necessary at the reduced airspeed to maintain wings level
Therefore, do not attempt to land with a crosswind from the side of the deployed flap
The additional roll control to counteract the crosswind may not be available
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
The wing with the retracted flap will stall much earlier - possible crossed control stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher-than-normal airspeed
Pressurization Malfunction
Not applicable for the Piper Arrow, but in general descend or use supplemental oxygen
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
Understanding different emergencies and how to deal with them is obviously important as you will always be prepared and be able to react quickly in the event one of these emergencies occurs.

paragraphs.text: XII.D. Emergency Equipment & Survival Gear
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story

Would you want to crash land in the desert with a life raft, life preserver, warm clothes, and an average water supply as your survival equipment? Or wouldn’t you rather have survival gear tailored to the flight you are taking? We want to be properly prepared for an emergency landing.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Emergency equipment and survival gear refers to the equipment that should be carried onboard an airplane based on the flight being taken to aid in survival and rescue operations.
Why
By carrying and understanding flight tailored survival equipment you will greatly increase odds of survival & rescue.
How:
Appropriate Equipment 										AI.XII.D.K3
For flight over uninhabited land areas, it is wise to take and know how to use survival equipment for the type of climate and terrain
Basic plan is equipment and gear for 48-72 hours, adjust as required
A survival kit should provide sustenance, shelter, medical care, and a means to summon help
Consider the area and how long you may be stranded
Consider the terrain, the climate/season, and type of emergency communication equipment needed
Mountainous terrain in December requires different survival gear than coastal flying in August
Flying over the Midwest US poses different threats than a coastal flight
If a forced landing occurs at sea, chances for survival are governed by the degree of proficiency in emergency procedures and by the availability and effectiveness of water survival equipment
General items to consider
More specific items should be considered based on the type of terrain and wildlife
Climate Extremes 										AI.XII.D.K3a
Cold
Warm clothes and layers, gloves, headgear, boots, snowshoes
Waterproof layer(s)
Blanket(s)
Shovel
Hand/body warmers
Hot
Light clothing & hat (sun protection), sunglasses, sunscreen, extra water
Mountainous Terrain 									AI.XII.D.K3b
Mosquito head net
Hiking boots
Warm/Cold weather clothing to adapt to temperature changes
Bear spray, or similar items depending on the wildlife
Overwater 											AI.XII.D.K3c
Life vests, Dry suit/survival suit
Raft
Think outside the box
What parts of the airplane/baggage could be used for survival?
Ex: The aircraft cover could be used for shelter, warmth, etc.
Equipment Use and Care
Onboard emergency equipment can often consist of an ELT, a fire extinguisher, emergency axe, and the survival gear you have packed
ELT 												AI.XII.D.K1
Purpose - transmit a downed aircraft’s location for search and rescue personnel
Broadcast on emergency frequencies of 121.5 and 243.0 (no longer monitored by satellite) and 406 MHz on newer ELTs
Operation/Use – If “armed” and when subject to crash-generated forces, ELTs are designed to automatically activate and continuously emit their respective signals, analog or digital
Transmitters will operate continuously for at least 48 hours over a wide temperature range
A properly installed, maintained, and functioning ELT can expedite search and rescue operations and save lives if it survives the crash and is activated (especially 406 MHz transponders)
Pilots/passengers should know how to activate the aircraft's ELT if manual activation is required
Be able to verify the ELT is functioning/transmitting an alert
Servicing - Must be checked every 12 calendar months
FAR 91.207 – The battery must be replaced after 1-hour cumulative use or ½ its useful life
ELT Testing
Analog 121.5/243 MHz ELTs – Test only during the first 5 minutes after any hour
If operational tests must be made outside of this period, they should be coordinated with the nearest FAA Control Tower
Tests should be no longer than three audible sweeps
Digital 406 MHz ELTs – Test in accordance with the unit's manufacturer's instructions
Airborne tests are not permitted
Storage – The ELT must be attached to the airplane in such a manner that the probability of damage to the transmitter in the case of a crash is minimized
Fixed/deployable automatic transmitters must be attached to the airplane as far aft as practical
Fire Extinguisher 										AI.XII.D.K2
Purpose - Used to fight/extinguish fires
Operation – Usually, pull the pin, point and squeeze the handle to spray
Adjust based on operating instructions
Aim at the base of the fire
Servicing – Verify the extinguisher isn’t expired, has been inspected, and contains the proper charge
Storage – Ensure it is attached/secured where it is supposed to be, securely in its mount
The last thing you need is to have to find the fire extinguisher during a fire
Emergency Axe
Purpose – To provide a means to exit in case the doors cannot be opened
Operation – If the door(s) cannot be opened, use the emergency axe to break through the canopy
In some aircraft, the axe can be used to cut through a portion of the fuselage
An axe is also a great addition to your survival gear
Servicing – Ensure the axe is onboard and properly mounted, and inspected as required
Storage – The axe should be stored in its mount as the manufacturer intends
RM: Survival Gear (for 48-72 hours) 								AI.XII.D.R1
Purpose – Used for survival (food, water, shelter, warmth, etc.)
Operation/Use – The operation/use will vary by equipment. Use based on the instructions
Servicing – Verify the equipment is in good working order and does not need to be replaced, cleaned, etc.
Ensure electronic equipment is in good working order and properly charged/ready for use
Adjust the contents of the survival gear based on the trip, weather, terrain, etc.
Storage – Store the gear safely and accessibly on the airplane
Ballistic Parachute 											AI.XII.D.K4
Provides an alternative to certain emergency situations
Parachute is deployed from the aircraft
Allows the airplane to descend slowly enough toward the ground such that occupants usually survive the impact with minor or no injuries
Understand and follow the procedures for arming/disarming and conditions under which it should be used
Conditions for Deployment
Examples include:
Catastrophic loss of controllability due to a collision or mechanical failure
Pilot incapacitation
Loss of control
Airframe will be lost, but if deployed in an acceptable flight regime it can prevent injuries & save lives
Passenger Brief
RM: Conditions for a safe deployment 							AI.XII.D.R2
When & How to deploy it
What to expect
Applicable hazards (Ex. Ground hazards with a deployed parachute, surface winds)
Evacuation procedures once on the ground
Instructor ACS Appendix 3 XII.D.
Follow the manufacturer’s procedures for arming/disarming the system before and after flight
Knowledge testing may include simulation and briefing of procedures but not actual deployment
Emergency Autoland (EAL) Systems 								AI.XII.D.K5
Designed to be deployed in the case of pilot incapacitation
How it Works
Manually activated by a pilot or passenger
Automatic Activation
If the system sense erratic flying, it stabilizes the aircraft, and checks for pilot responsiveness
Without further input, it initiates an emergency descent
If no further input, it initiates the process for an automated landing
Transmits automated messages on the last selected frequency and Guard & squawks 7700
Call sign and intention to divert to a particular airport and runway
Passenger Brief
RM: Conditions for a safe deployment 							AI.XII.D.R3
When & How to deploy it
What to expect
Evacuation procedures on the ground
Any applicable hazards
FAA Safety Team Emergency Autoland Overview
Common Errors 											AI.XII.D.K6
Failure to carry appropriate gear & equipment for the route of flight
Failure to maintain the equipment/gear
Lack of understanding of the operation and use of emergency gear & equipment
Failure to understand when and how to deploy emergency systems (i.e., parachute & Autoland)
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

Emergency equipment should be tailored to the type of flight that will be taken. Gear should be stored and serviced properly to ensure it functions properly during an emergency. Survival manuals can be obtained to help in planning.

text_content: A maneuver for descending as rapidly as possible to a lower altitude, or to the ground for an emergency landing
The need for this maneuver may result from an uncontrollable fire, a sudden loss of cabin pressurization, or any other situation demanding an immediate and rapid descent for survival
Descend as soon and as rapidly as possible within the structural limitations of the airplane
Set the propeller to low pitch (high rpm)
General procedures listed above, adjust based on the POH
Lower the nose to maintain maximum allowable airspeed
Never exceed VNE or VFE, or VA in turbulence
Puts positive load on the aircraft
Gets the airplane off an airway
Technique: Left turn since faster traffic passes on the right
Smoothly level off to prevent overstressing the airplane
Lead the level off by 10% of the VSI
In a real-life emergency descent, do what is necessary to land safely & stay alive
Increase power to the cruise setting, or as required
Once straight-and-level and accelerating, return to a normal configuration
May not be necessary if continuing directly into an emergency landing
In the case the engine fails, remaining altitude dictates the distance you can travel
Headwind decreases distance traveled, tailwind increases distance
Landing: Max demonstrated crosswind & landing distance required with a tailwind
Preflight Planning: Know safe altitudes & Max Elevation Figures
Especially important at high rates of descent
The farther the emergency descent is extended, the less glide distance available
Terminate the descent at an altitude that ensures a precautionary/emergency landing
Consequences of failing to identify reason for executing an emergency descent
Improper use of the prescribed emergency checklist
Improper use of clearing procedures for initiating the emergency descent
Improper procedures for recovering from an emergency descent
Series of short regularly spaced eye movements
Emergency Descent: Use the descending turn to clear for traffic
Clearly communicate intentions & location in the practice area
Turn on landing lights during takeoff & below 10,000’ MSL
Be aware of hazardous terrain around the airfield/practice area
Use Maximum Elevation Figures and other data
Anywhere: Altitude allowing emergency landing without undue hazard
Congested: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Be familiar with any obstacles nearby airports
Supporting guy wires can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Transmission lines often span departures and landmarks pilots follow
Be alert for anyone or anything that may cause a hazard
Taxiing: Stop until safe to proceed
If it’s a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance and clear for traffic
If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it

If SA or orientation is lost, admit it, and fix it
Level-off altitude, emergency & associated procedures, configuration, & the plan

Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating

text_content: A simulated emergency landing occurs when the power is pulled, simulating a lost engine, and the pilot must attempt to restart the engine while properly configuring for an approach and landing, usually in a nearby field
To develop accuracy, judgment, planning, technique, and confidence when little or no engine power is available
Speed at which the aircraft glides the furthest for the least altitude lost in non-powered flight
Glide Ratio: Distance the airplane travels in relation to the altitude it loses
Provides estimate of how far you can fly
Any speed above or below Best Glide reduces the glide ratio
Best glide airspeed increases with weight
L/D determines the distance an airplane can glide
A heavier plane needs to fly at a higher speed to obtain the same L/DMAX & the glide ratio
The heavier plane will travel the same distance as the lighter plane, but in a shorter time
Tailwind: Higher groundspeed so the aircraft glides farther than with no wind
Headwind: Lower groundspeed and the aircraft does not glide as far as with no wind
When drag increases, the airplane must be pitched down to maintain airspeed
Minimize drag-producing components to maximize glide distance
Airspeed used to maximize the time that the airplane remains in flight
Results in losing altitude at the lowest rate
Less distance traveled compared to best glide speed
Generally, a few knots less than best glide airspeed
DO NOT attempt to stretch a glide by increasing back pressure & slowing below best glide
Any speed other than best glide reduces distance traveled
